items.title: The Cynicism of Trump’s Climate Policy
items.description: President Trump has previously called climate change a “hoax” and a “scam.” But last month, when the Environmental Protection Agency proposed rescinding the conclusion that greenhouse-gas emissions from the power sector “may reasonably be anticipated to endanger public health or welfare,” it did not question the reality of climate change. Instead, it claimed that large emissions reductions will not be enough to avert harm, and the country is better off doing nothing at all. This is utter nihilism. It is also completely wrong. The power sector is the second largest emitter of greenhouse gases in the United States (only transportation emits more), accounting for approximately 24 percent of the country’s emissions. The U.S., in turn, is the second largest emitter of greenhouse gases in the world, after China, accounting for approximately 12 percent of the global total. If the U.S. power sector were a country, it would be the sixth largest emitter of greenhouse gases (fifth if European Union countries were counted individually rather than as a single jurisdiction). The EPA’s argument is similar to one the agency made in February, when it said that eliminating such emissions from the transportation sector would likewise not make an appreciable difference. Putting these two claims together magnifies the brazenness: The EPA argues that eliminating or substantially reducing about half of U.S. greenhouse-gas emissions would be futile and would not meaningfully slow the pace of climate change. It follows from the EPA’s logic that eliminating or substantially reducing the greenhouse-gas emissions of any other sector of the economy would be even more pointless. And the same goes for the emissions of any sector of any country, anywhere in the world. In fact, according to the EPA’s reasoning, nothing anyone could do anywhere would make any difference. (It also, relatedly, makes a legal claim that it doesn’t have the authority to regulate greenhouse-gas emissions in the first place.) The agency’s approach is akin to saying that eating a whole loaf of bread is calorie-free as long as the bread is cut in sufficiently thin slices—they’re all so thin that they can’t possibly matter. [ Read: What does the climate movement do now? ] These are standards I know well. From January 2023 to January 2025, when I served as the administrator of the White House Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs, I was responsible for the review of all significant executive-branch regulations, including this one. The fact is that some of those slices are not thin at all. The U.S. power sector’s greenhouse-gas emissions create enormous damage . In 2022, the power sector emitted more than 1.5 billion tons of carbon dioxide, more than 68,000 tons of nitrous oxide, and more than 35,000 tons of methane, all three of which are powerful greenhouse gases. Reducing this pollution—and the climate and health damages it creates—would greatly benefit life on Earth. The global advantages of the EPA’s carbon-pollution standards, which the Biden administration announced in 2024 and the Trump administration now seeks to repeal, were estimated to be $20 billion a year—a total that includes savings both from avoiding climate change and from reducing localized pollution that harms human health. Of this total, several billion dollars’ worth of avoided economic damages would accrue to Americans specifically. A report by the Institute for Policy Integrity estimated that one year’s worth of greenhouse-gas emissions from the U.S. power sector would produce roughly 5,300 additional yearly premature deaths from heat waves and wildfires in the U.S. alone. This figure does not include the significant number of additional deaths from co-pollutants, such as particulate matter, that power plants emit. Putting the magnitude of this effect in context, the report noted that 5,300 deaths are “more than the annual U.S. deaths caused by kidney infections, the flu, firearm accidents, meningitis, bronchitis, appendicitis, and salmonella combined.” In its proposed repeal of emissions limits, the EPA ignores these effects. Instead, the agency presents an estimate showing that even if the greenhouse-gas emissions of the U.S. power sector were eliminated, the impacts on global mean surface temperature and sea-level rise would be small. The agency wholly ignores the scientific evidence that increased weather-pattern volatility, such as storm surges, not averages of measurements such as temperature, drives most negative impacts of climate change. The EPA’s approach is like saying that an office building is comfortable if its mean temperature is 70 degrees, without checking whether some rooms are at 90 degrees and others at 50 degrees. The EPA has no good arguments to call the existing evidence into question. The Biden administration’s process to determine the economic damages from greenhouse gases unfolded over several years, and included robust public input and peer review. The EPA casts all of this aside in three steps: First, it acknowledges (against its own interest) that, under the relevant provision of the Clean Air Act, “the appropriate indicator of impact is not emissions or concentrations, but public health and welfare impacts.” Second, although this would suggest that negative consequences of rescinding endangerment findings would be measured by additional forecasted deaths, for example, the EPA in fact does not consider any such impacts. Third, the EPA waves aside all estimates of such consequences using just one word: uncertainties . In its view, uncertainty renders careful estimates of future damages completely invalid. [ Read: Climate change is moving mountains ] Hiding behind uncertainties is a cruel trick that the Trump administration has used with abandon. In multiple proceedings from February onward, it has cited “uncertainties” as a reason to stop estimating the local damage from dangerous air pollutants, such as particulate matter and ozone. For decades, those estimates had been provided on the basis of extensive peer-reviewed scientific literature, but the EPA now essentially assumes that this pollution causes no negative health effects, because whatever consequences existed were too “uncertain.” One curiosity: In proposing the rescission of the endangerment finding, the agency does not dispute the seriousness of climate change. The proposal discusses at some length a July study by the National Academy of Sciences on the attribution of extreme weather events to global climate change—a study well within the mainstream of climate science. The EPA does not take issue with the academy’s study and is therefore implicitly saying that climate change is a serious problem, but that it can do nothing to ameliorate the severely negative consequences. But this too is wrong. Of course, the benefits of U.S. emissions reductions would be augmented if they were accompanied by correspondingly ambitious actions by other countries. If the U.S. believed that other countries were not doing enough on that front, instead of rescinding its own restrictions, it could use its considerable power on the world stage to induce other countries to do more. The Trump administration is doing the opposite: It withdrew from the Paris Agreement, under which countries, including the United States, pledged to meet emissions-reduction targets, and it stopped participating in international climate negotiations altogether. The Trump administration is not merely cynical; it is also irrational and wrong. If its nihilism becomes our national policy, as it is proposing, everyone will suffer the consequences.

items.title: American Sustenance
items.description: When I first set out to report and write about what we now call the food system, I ran into a brick wall with editors in New York. This was in the late 1990s and early aughts. I was chasing stories about the new genetically modified crops, the fight over the federal definition of organic , and the rise of gigantic factory farms—stories that would eventually find their way into my book The Omnivore’s Dilemma —but few editors seemed interested. At first I was baffled. I had read my Wendell Berry and had taken to heart his famous dictum, “Eating is an agriculture act.” Didn’t everybody know that? A century or so ago, the question of where our food comes from would have been too obvious to pose, let alone investigate and write a book about. In 1900, about four of every 10 Americans were farmers, and everyone else was likely related to one. But as the food chains that fed us grew longer and more intricate, they became invisible to most of us, to the point where urban Americans seemed satisfied with the answer “Food comes from the supermarket.” For cosmopolitan Americans around the turn of the millennium, the seemingly obvious connection between agriculture and eating was not obvious at all. Maybe that was my problem! “Agriculture” was a distant and musty abstraction, something that happens in I states such as Iowa and Indiana, and was of no conceivable interest to urban readers. I revised my pitches, dropped the word agriculture , which to the typical editor in New York might as well have been something that happens in Alpha Centauri, and replaced it with food . Instead of pitching a piece about factory farms, for instance, I proposed a story about “how a prime cut of beef finds its way from a pasture in South Dakota to a steakhouse in New York.” It worked, almost like magic. Who isn’t interested in food? It turned out that editors in New York were especially keen on it; many of them were foodies and, at least in those days, had healthy expense accounts. [ Read: The dark history of how coffee took over the world ] Mine wasn’t the only or even the first such book: Eric Schlosser’s Fast Food Nation (2001) and Marion Nestle’s Food Politics (2002) had come out a few years before. All three books sought to connect a series of far­-flung dots: between the way we farm and the way we eat, but also between industrial agriculture and obesity (and chronic disease); farm policy and the environmental crisis; the rise of fast food and the collapse of home cooking; monoculture farming and fossil fuels; concentration in the food industry and the hollowing-out of rural America. Another concept you hardly ever heard about back then was “food politics,” as Marion reminded me recently. When in the early 2000s she told the dean of her school at New York University the title of her latest book, he wrinkled his brow and asked, “What does food have to do with politics?” (“No one ever asks me that question anymore,” Marion recently pointed out.) Food has become a political issue. In the years after The Omnivore’s Dilemma came out, in 2006, something that looked very much like a movement began to take shape. True, it never coalesced around any single issue. For better or worse, the food movement was and remains a baggy coalition of a great many groups pushing a great many different issues: fighting food insecurity, curbing pesticide use, reforming farm policy, promoting farmers’ markets, advancing farmworker and food-worker rights, passing stiffer food-safety laws, promoting animal welfare, and so on. These factions sometimes work at cross­-purposes. For example, activists working to strengthen food-safety rules sometimes run afoul of local food advocates, who worry that the burden of new regulations will hinder the revival of small­-farm agriculture. Still, to watch so much activism galvanize around food and farming filled many of us with hope that things might actually change. For me, the high­-water mark of that hope came during the 2008 presidential campaign, when Barack Obama gave an interview to Time magazine in which he referenced my critique of the food system. Because “our entire agricultural system is built on cheap oil,” he said, “our agriculture sector actually is contributing more greenhouse gases than our transportation sector. And in the meantime, it’s creating monocultures that are vulnerable to national security threats, are now vulnerable to sky­-high food prices or crashes in food prices, huge swings in commodity prices, and are partly responsible for the explosion in our health care costs because they’re contributing to Type 2 diabetes, stroke and heart disease, obesity.” Could the nascent food movement have found a powerful new champion? It certainly seemed that way. Obama campaigned aggressively in Iowa, promising to stand up to Big Food and vowing to regulate concentrated animal feeding operations, or CAFOs, “just as any other polluter.” On the campaign trail, as I’ve previously written , he told Iowans that they had a right to know where in the world their food came from and whether it had been genetically modified. To critics of the food system, the Obama campaign gave many of us hope that we would have an ally in the White House. (By the way, Obama won Iowa—twice!—the last Democrat to do so.) But as the candidate and the movement soon learned, the power of agribusiness is formidable. A few short days after his interview with Time , Senator Charles Grassley, a.k.a. the Senior Senator From Corn, seized on Obama’s Time interview as evidence that he was blaming farmers for obesity and pollution. A campaign spokesman played down Obama’s remarks, saying he had simply been “paraphrasing” something he’d read. The episode taught Obama and the rest of us a painful lesson about just what we were up against with Big Food. Once in the White House, the Obamas occasionally nurtured the hopes of food reformers. In the spring of 2009, Michelle Obama planted an organic vegetable garden on the White House lawn. The small patch excited the food movement but brought down the wrath of the chemical industry. Chemical-industry groups labeled the Obamas “organic limousine liberals” while an agribusiness trade organization called on the first lady to use pesticides in her garden, never mind that she had no need for them. The dustup was a preview of things to come: Whatever steps the Obamas took to reform the food system would be met by ferocious attacks from industry—and, alas, would all too often result in retreat by the administration. Although Michelle did notch a significant victory with the Healthy, Hunger-Free Kids Act of 2010, which made meaningful reforms to the school-lunch program—reforms that the first Trump administration has rolled back. [ Read: One food all Americans can agree on ] Big Food’s favorite line of attack? Depicting efforts to improve the food system as “elitist,” leading America down the path to a “nanny state.” The charge of elitism stung, not least because it contained more than a kernel of truth. The food movement has been mainly a coastal phenomenon, attracting the well­-heeled and well­ educated who could afford to buy sustainably and humanely grown food. Many of the changes the movement sought—such as tighter regulation of factory farms and pesticides, higher pay for food workers, and rules favoring organic agriculture and grass­-fed meat—threatened to increase the price of food. This fact, I think, sharply circumscribed the movement’s power and appeal. Cheap food—which stands as the single great accomplishment of the industrial food system—is bound to be politically popular, even if that cheap food comes at a very high price to our health and the health of our planet, not to mention to the taxpayers footing the bill for crop subsidies. And food has become dramatically more expensive since the Obama years. Americans are living through the biggest jump in grocery prices in half a century; prices have climbed by roughly 33 percent since 2019 alone. Since at least the French Revolution, politicians have been very fond of cheap food, and understandably so. The legacy of the Obamas’ engagement with food issues has been to make clear to anyone paying attention that food is political, a matter of public debate, and is likely to become more so in the future. How do we know that? Because it will be difficult, if not impossible, to address the climate crisis without addressing the carbon footprint of industrial agriculture—and difficult, if not impossible, to address the explosion in health-care costs without addressing the American diet, which contributes to many of the chronic diseases that most of our health-care dollars go to treat. Twenty years after the publication of The Omnivore’s Dilemma , you might think—and I certainly hoped!—that my book would have fallen hopelessly out of date. But looking at the landscape of food and farming today, I’m sorry to report that things haven’t changed all that much. King Corn still rules the American heartland, where 95 million acres are dedicated to that single crop, up from 78 million acres when the book was first published. Chemically intensive monoculture farming remains the rule, encouraged by lavish federal subsidies that discourage farmers from trying anything else. The American taxpayer continues to subsidize the least healthy calories in the supermarket. Our government is backing both sides in the war against type 2 diabetes and obesity, spending billions to treat these chronic diseases while subsidizing the crop that gives us high­-fructose corn syrup. Corn remains the essential building block of the food Americans eat; along with soy, its partner in the fields, it gets turned into the meat and dairy and processed foods that dominate the American diet. Meanwhile, the small number of corporations that dominate meatpacking, seed production, chemical fertilizers and pesticides, grain trading and processing, fast-food chains, and supermarkets has only gotten smaller since 2006, as oligopolies tighten their grip on the industrial food chain that feeds most of us. But not all the news is dire. Some things have changed for the better. Americans are paying more attention to what they eat—both the food’s healthfulness (or lack thereof) and its provenance. Many of us have opted out of the industrial-food economy. Today, you can find organic food in virtually every supermarket; organic is now a thriving $65 billion industry (up from roughly $13 billion in 2005). Add to that the market for local food—the Department of Agriculture estimates that there are now more than 8,100 farmers’ markets in America (up from about 4,000 in 2005) and another 7,200 CSAs, or subscription farms—plus all the animal products labeled grass-fed or humanely raised, and you have an alternative food economy easily approaching $75 billion a year. While the government dithers, consumers are voting with their forks for a different kind of food system. Another important change since The Omnivore’s Dilemma was published was the emergence of a word: ultra­-processed , as in ultra­-processed foods. The term does not appear in the book, because it wasn’t used to describe a particular type of food until 2009. It was introduced by Carlos Monteiro, a Brazilian epidemiologist, who had been puzzling over a paradox: Brazilians were getting fatter and more diabetic and yet, as a population, they were eating roughly the same quantities of fat, carbohydrates, and protein. He investigated and discovered that what had changed was the form in which people were consuming these nutrients. In place of traditional dishes, they were consuming more ready-to-eat meals, snack foods, and soda. He dubbed these products “ultra­-processed,” which he defined as ready­-to­-eat foods you can’t make at home, because they require a factory and a suite of ingredients—including additives, dyes, and emulsifiers—that no ordinary person keeps in their pantry. (I call them “edible food­-like substances.”) Monteiro’s insight is a powerful one: that the form in which we get our nutrients—whether as traditional whole foods or highly processed food products—has a significant bearing on our health and weight. Subsequent research has shown that people who eat ultra­-processed foods end up consuming several hundred more calories a day than those who don’t. Consumption of these foods—most of which contain ingredients derived from corn and soy—has also been linked to several chronic diseases. How big a problem is ultra-processed food? Today it is the source of 55 percent of the calories in the American diet, and that figure is even higher for children—62 percent. Much to the dismay of the food industry, the term has broken through with the public. (Just the other night, I saw an ad on television for a brand of dog food that boasted it was “real food, not ultra­-processed.”) A poll taken in 2025 by a conservative think tank found that 70 percent of likely voters opposed serving ultra­-processed foods in school meals; 96 percent favored putting warning labels on such foods. The current secretary of health and human services, Robert F. Kennedy Jr., has no doubt driven up these numbers with his vow to get ultra­-processed foods out of the national school-lunch program. We shall see if Big Food lets him. [ Read: Fruit is too sweet ] But the secretary has at his back a large army of activists and voters who are changing the politics of food in ways that could help propel reform. I’m referring to the “Make America Healthy Again,” or MAHA, movement, which Kennedy helped galvanize and then brought into the Trump tent. This is potentially significant. As long as the food movement was coded liberal or left and vulnerable to charges of elitism, there was a ceiling on its political power. But now the people who are calling for a ban on certain pesticides and getting ultra­-processed foods out of the school-lunch program are the MAHA moms, and you no longer hear talk of elitism or the nanny state. I should have seen this coming. There’s a moment in The Omnivore’s Dilemma when I ask a farmer named Joel Salatin who his customers are. His Polyface Farm is one of the most radical in America, and he is a libertarian free spirit with no patience for government regulation or agricultural convention. He’s designed an intricate food chain that starts with sunlight and grass and supports half a dozen animal species living symbiotically. Who, I wondered, would schlep all the way to Swoope, Virginia, the remote, far­-off-the­-interstate burg where he farms, to buy his pastured chickens and grass-fed beef? He described young mothers concerned about the health of their children, many of them drawn from the homeschooling and homesteading community. “People who have already opted out once,” as Joel points out. I met some of these mothers the week I spent working on Joel’s farm. They held fierce views on nutrition that weren’t always aligned with science: Seed oils and grains were a problem; raw milk was a solution; “clean” food was medicine. These moms were deeply suspicious of institutions of all kinds, including food corporations, the medical system, and especially the FDA; they bridled against the agency’s food-safety rules. Many of these moms had kids with serious health issues that they hoped to address with a change in diet—hence their willingness to travel hundreds of miles to fill their coolers with Joel’s pastured meat and eggs. I didn’t know it at the time, but I was meeting future MAHA moms; it never occurred to me that they might coalesce into a movement that would have the ear of a president. Perhaps not surprisingly, Salatin has become a MAHA hero, invited to appear at rallies and brought in to consult with administration officials. He recently told me that the administration had reached out during the transition to gauge his interest in becoming the agriculture secretary. Imagine that! [ Read: MAHA is complicating one of the hardest parts of parenting ] It’s not at all clear what, if anything, will come of this new politics. The underlying DNA of MAHA is very different from the DNA of the first­-wave food movement. MAHA is fundamentally libertarian, allergic to the sort of government intervention that people in the earlier food movement consider necessary to build a healthier, more just, and sustainable food system. MAHA’s primary interest is our health as individuals, not the health of the environment; the movement has shown little interest in food insecurity or the rights of food workers. As Marion Nestle put it to me in an email, “The MAHA movement is like Joel Salatin. Everything up to the individual with little attention to policy.” And yet there are promising areas of overlap—around banning agricultural chemicals and the ingredients in ultra­-processed foods, as well as supporting local food systems and regenerative farming. The prospect that MAHA will get very far with an administration that regards all regulation as anathema seems doubtful. The Trump EPA is bent on deregulating agricultural chemicals, much to MAHA’s frustration, and the Trump USDA has been gutting support for small farms and local food systems. (It’s also worth pointing out that a diet of real food is not going to save children from the measles; what the Trump administration is doing to public health in America needs to be viewed in its totality.) What is encouraging, I think, is that a vocal constituency seeking reform of food and agriculture has emerged on the right, adding its numbers and energy to the earlier wave of food activism coming from the left. Should the Trump administration disappoint or frustrate the MAHA moms, as appears to be happening, they may well look to form alliances with groups that share their priorities. They are nothing if not fierce. Could a new, bipartisan, and far more powerful food movement be built upon these areas of overlap? Early this year, we saw the first evidence of the power of that alliance, when MAHA activists teamed up with Democratic Representative Chellie Pingree, a Maine organic farmer and a leader of the food movement, to strip a provision from an appropriations bill that would have shielded pesticide manufacturers from lawsuits. The building of coalitions like this one is surely cause for optimism. The demand for healthy food produced in a safe manner is something with the potential to unite us. Who can be against that kind of food? Only a powerful lobby, and one that has been very good at dividing us along lines of class and culture. But that strategy may no longer work, now that there are tens of millions of Americans on both sides of the ideological divide who recognize that our food system is badly broken, that it is responsible for our national eating disorder. This could be the start of something big. We can hope. This essay is adapted from the introduction to a new edition of The Omnivore’s Dilemma .

items.title: Guinée : le ministère de l’Environnement mobilise médias et leaders religieux dans la croisade contre les plastiques à usage unique
items.description: Le ministère de l’Environnement et du Développement Durable entend renforcer la sensibilisation contre les plastiques à usage unique en Guinée. À cet effet, un atelier de formation des acteurs clés s’est tenu le lundi 19 octobre 2026 au Centre national de perfectionnement de Donka, à Conakry. La rencontre a réuni des journalistes, des leaders religieux, des représentants de la société civile et des administrateurs de marchés autour des stratégies de lutte contre la pollution plastique. Présidant la cérémonie d’ouverture, le ministre de l’Environnement et du Développement Durable, Fassou Théa, a insisté sur la nécessité d’impliquer les relais d’opinion dans la sensibilisation des populations et le respect des mesures d’interdiction des plastiques à usage unique en vigueur en Guinée. Selon lui, l’accumulation des déchets plastiques dans les quartiers, les marchés, les caniveaux et les cours d’eau constitue une préoccupation collective. Cette situation contribue à la dégradation de l’environnement et aggrave les risques d’inondation, notamment pendant la saison des fortes pluies. « Notre responsabilité est de faire connaître les dispositions en vigueur et d’en favoriser le respect », a-t-il déclaré, soulignant que leur application nécessite une information claire, un dialogue avec les acteurs concernés et l’adhésion des citoyens. Des relais d’opinion au cœur de la sensibilisation Le ministre a mis en avant le rôle complémentaire des différentes catégories de participants dans cette démarche. Les médias sont appelés à éclairer le débat public et à diffuser des informations fiables, tandis que les leaders religieux peuvent relayer les messages de protection de l’environnement à travers leurs prêches. Les organisations de la société civile et les administrateurs de marchés sont également invités à renforcer les échanges avec les populations et les commerçants afin de favoriser une meilleure compréhension des mesures prises contre les plastiques à usage unique. Fassou Théa a toutefois reconnu que l’abandon de ces produits nécessite des adaptations pour les producteurs, les commerçants et les consommateurs. Il a ainsi plaidé en faveur de solutions de remplacement accessibles et adaptées aux besoins des populations, tout en encourageant les initiatives locales. Le ministre a souhaité que les travaux débouchent sur des messages de sensibilisation adaptés aux différents publics et sur des actions concrètes assorties de mécanismes de suivi. Avant de déclarer ouverts les travaux de l’atelier, il a également appelé à une meilleure coordination entre les participants, les collectivités et les services compétents afin d’étendre cette mobilisation à l’ensemble du territoire national. Des propositions adaptées aux réalités du terrain Au cours de la formation, les participants ont pris part à des travaux de groupe consacrés aux moyens de renforcer la sensibilisation contre l’utilisation des plastiques à usage unique. Ces échanges leur ont permis de formuler des propositions tenant compte de leurs domaines d’intervention respectifs et des réalités du terrain. Les discussions ont notamment porté sur les stratégies de communication susceptibles de mieux informer les populations sur les conséquences environnementales et sanitaires des déchets plastiques, ainsi que sur la réglementation en vigueur. Les journalistes appelés à contribuer au changement de comportement Parmi les participantes, M’Ballou Fatoumata Souaré, journaliste reporter au journal Le Punch a souligné l’importance du rôle des médias dans la lutte contre la pollution plastique. Elle estime que cette formation lui a permis de mieux appréhender les enjeux liés aux plastiques à usage unique et leurs conséquences sur l’environnement. Selon elle, la mission des journalistes ne se limite pas à informer : ils doivent également contribuer à sensibiliser les populations et à encourager l’adoption de comportements responsables. La journaliste entend mettre ses compétences au service de cette cause à travers des articles, des reportages et des campagnes de sensibilisation sur les réseaux sociaux. Elle souhaite également contribuer à rendre les informations environnementales plus accessibles, notamment aux jeunes. À travers cette initiative, le ministère de l’Environnement et du Développement durable mise sur l’engagement des acteurs institutionnels et communautaires pour renforcer la lutte contre la pollution plastique et favoriser des changements durables dans les habitudes de consommation.

items.title: Obuasi SHTS sex scandal: NAGRAT demands dismissal of headmaster, district GES officials
items.description: The President of the National Association of Graduate Teachers (NAGRAT), Jacob Anaba, has called for the immediate dismissal of the headmaster of Obuasi Senior High Technical School (SHTS), Zakaria Abdulai, and officials of the Ghana Education Service (GES) in the area in relation to allegations of sexual abuse of female students. The headmaster is at the centre of the alleged sexual abuse scandal in Joy News investigative correspondent Manasseh Azure Awuni’s documentary, Inside the Dreaded Headmaster’s Bungalow. The documentary captures over 14 alleged sexual abuse cases involving female students at the Obuasi Senior High Technical School. Commenting on the scandal, Mr Anaba accused education officials in the Obuasi district of being aware of the complaints filed against the headmaster but failing to take decisive action, arguing that those responsible for protecting students should be held accountable for their poor handling of the matter. “All those people heading the GES in that office, they should go. All of them, they are complicit. All of them,” Mr Anaba said on Joy News’ PM Express on Monday, October 19. “In the Obuasi districts, the head of the district, all of them should go, because they are aware of this situation. They shouldn’t have allowed this thing to happen.” Mr Anaba said reports about the alleged abuse dated back to 2025, raising questions about why the concerns had not triggered an effective response before the issue became public. He said students and parents had complained before the matter attracted widespread attention, adding that the anger of students had helped bring it into the public domain. “It was the wrath of the students that brought this thing into the public domain. It happened earlier before that,” he said. ‘No one should be shielded’ The NAGRAT president questioned the response of local officials, including the district officials, whom he alleged had known about the complaints but failed to take appropriate action. He insisted that anyone found to have failed in their duties or committed an offence should face the appropriate consequences, regardless of their position or professional standing. “You see, this Ghana belongs to all of us. We have to protect the Ghana that we all belong to,” he said. “So, if a member of us, a teacher, does the wrong thing, he must be taken through the due course of the law. No one should be shielded. No one.” Mr Anaba argued that the teaching profession carried a special responsibility because of the trust placed in teachers and school authorities by students and their families. He said the headmaster should not be allowed to continue teaching if the allegations against him were established. “This man should leave immediately. He can’t be a teacher again, because the profession that we decide to belong to is a noble one,” he said. “You have a fiduciary relationship with the student that you are handling. We may make mistakes, but not this type of mistake.” 38 teachers reportedly asked to leave The NAGRAT leader further revealed that 38 teachers at the Obuasi Senior High Technical School (SHTS) were asked to leave the school after speaking out against the headmaster’s conduct. He was concerned that teachers who sought to protect the interests of the affected students were rather being victimised, with their jobs on the line. “As I speak to you, 38 teachers were being asked to leave the school. What was the reason?” he asked. Mr Anaba alleged that the directive followed the work of a fact-finding committee chaired by the district director of education, who, he said, had instructed the assistant headmaster to communicate the decision to the teachers. The headmaster has reportedly been interdicted and suspended following the latest revelations as investigations intensify.

items.title: Mondial 2026: la FIFA suspend trois cadres de l’Égypte
items.description: La FIFA a infligé jusqu’à cinq matches de suspension au sélectionneur égyptien Hossam Hassan, au directeur de la sélection, Ibrahim Hassan, et à l’attaquant Mostafa Ziko, à la suite des déclarations et des incidents ayant entouré le huitième de finale perdu contre l’Argentine (3-2). Ces sanctions risquent de peser sur la préparation des Pharaons pour les qualifications à la CAN 2027. La Fédération égyptienne de football (FEF) a annoncé, lundi 19 octobre 2026, avoir reçu notification des sanctions disciplinaires prononcées par la Fédération internationale de football association (FIFA) contre trois membres de la sélection nationale. Hossam Hassan et Ibrahim Hassan écopent chacun de trois matches de suspension, tandis que Mostafa Ziko est sanctionné de cinq rencontres. À l’origine de ces mesures figurent les déclarations et les incidents ayant entouré l’élimination de l’Égypte face à l’Argentine en huitièmes de finale de la Coupe du Monde 2026. Avant la rencontre, le sélectionneur égyptien avait exprimé son soutien à la Palestine. Après la défaite de son équipe, il avait également dénoncé un traitement de faveur accordé à l’Argentine et un manque d’équité dans la compétition. Ces sanctions auront des répercussions sur les prochaines échéances internationales des Pharaons. Les trois hommes manqueront les deux rencontres contre le Malawi, prévues le mois prochain dans le cadre des éliminatoires de la Coupe d’Afrique des nations (CAN) 2027. Hossam Hassan et son frère Ibrahim seront également absents lors du premier match de la sélection égyptienne en mars 2027, face à l’Angola. La sanction visant Mostafa Ziko est plus sévère. Selon les informations communiquées, l’attaquant sera éloigné des terrains jusqu’en juin prochain. Il manquera ainsi les quatre dernières rencontres de l’Égypte dans les qualifications pour la CAN 2027, ainsi qu’un autre match. Avant de rendre ses décisions, la commission de discipline de la FIFA avait ouvert une enquête sur les propos tenus par les trois hommes après la confrontation face à l’Argentine. Cette procédure a finalement débouché sur les suspensions désormais notifiées à la fédération égyptienne. La Fédération égyptienne réclame des explications. Elle a officiellement saisi la commission de discipline de la FIFA afin d’obtenir les motifs et les justifications détaillées de ces sanctions. Une démarche qui pourrait permettre à l’instance nationale de mieux comprendre les fondements des décisions prises contre trois membres de la sélection. Par Valentin SOMANDE L’article Mondial 2026: la FIFA suspend trois cadres de l’Égypte est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: SDP to scrap bulletproof SUVs, charter jets for officials – Adebayo
items.description: By John Alechenu, Abuja Presidential candidate of the Social Democratic Party, SDP, Prince Adewole Adebayo, has declared that an SDP-led administration will end the current system where ordinary citizens subsidise the lavish lifestyles of public officials. Speaking through a press release signed by Comrade Mark Adebayo, Chief Media and Communications Advisor of the Adebayo-Bugaje Presidential Campaign, the SDP candidate said his government will redirect trillions of Naira currently wasted on luxury items into education, healthcare and critical infrastructure. “We will stop Nigerians from subsidizing the lavish lifestyles of politicians,” Adebayo stated. He stressed that “the widespread economic hardship across the country is not due to a lack of resources but rather the result of a ruling class that prioritizes institutionalized waste over human capital development.” Adebayo critiqued the current political culture, noting that “successive budgets have systematically funnelled enormous public capital into executive comforts while millions of families deal with inflation, fuel duty increases, and crumbling social services.” Citing fiscal estimates from civil society tracking reports, budget analyses and state-level disclosures, the campaign said the cost of political opulence runs into multiple trillions of Naira annually. According to the statement, recent federal reviews indicate that nearly ₦1 trillion is regularly earmarked or spent across cycles on luxury utility vehicles, presidential fleet upgrades, State House renovations, and loosely defined regional empowerment schemes for political aides. It added that mid-2026 budget implementation data shows that just 33 state governments expended over $300 million, about ₦410 billion, on governors’ offices, Government Houses and executive travels within six months, pointing to an annual state-level lifestyle drain exceeding ₦1 Trillion across all 36 states. “If what we read from independent tracking of state and federal agencies by concerned NGOs and experts are of any substance, we consider consistent multi-billion Naira deviations for luxury armor vehicles, such as recent single-agency procurements exceeding ₦10 Billion for official management fleets, alongside state governments buying luxury vehicles entirely outside standard appropriation bills as criminal wastes in the midst of mass suffering induced by the anti-people policies of the current APC administration,” the statement said. Adebayo emphasised that under an SDP administration, these multi-trillion Naira leakages will be completely plugged. He maintained that four years is sufficient for a determined, transparent leader to restructure public finances, eliminate unconstitutional vehicle allowances and deliver functional infrastructure, matching historical benchmarks of focused governance in Nigeria. The SDP candidate urged Nigerians to reject the cycle of voting for leaders who treat public resources as personal accounts, reaffirming the party’s commitment to an economic system focused on public welfare, domestic production and transparent service delivery. The post SDP to scrap bulletproof SUVs, charter jets for officials – Adebayo appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.description: El Tribunal Supremo ha aplicado la amnistía al exvicepresidente de la Generalitat Oriol Junqueras y a los exconsejeros Raül Romeva, Dolors Bassa y Jordi Turull. Dos semanas después de que el Tribunal Constitucional estableciera que la Sala Penal debió otorgar la medida de gracia al delito de malversación que atribuyó a los exdirigentes independentistas, el Supremo ha cumplido ese mandato y ha amnistiado a los cuatro antiguos miembros del Govern a los que juzgó y condenó por ese delito en 2019. La amnistía deja sin efecto la pena de inhabilitación que aún pesaba sobre ellos, por lo que los cuatro podrían ya presentarse a las próximas elecciones u ocupar un cargo público. En el auto en el que expone su decisión, el Supremo lanza al Constitucional un reproche insólito, por extenso y contundente. “Su innecesaria grandilocuencia revela el deseo de adornar un razonamiento invasivo del ámbito jurisdiccional que corresponde al Tribunal Supremo”, recalcan los jueces. items.title: Deux soldats ukrainiens auraient saboté les gazoducs Nord Stream 1 et 2
items.description: Un procès historique s'est ouvert devant un tribunal à Hambourg, en Allemagne : Serhii Kuznetsov, un soldat des forces spéciales ukrainiennes est accusé d’avoir saboté, en septembre 2022, les gazoducs sous-marins Nord Stream 1 et 2 en mer Baltique, qui approvisionnent l’Allemagne en gaz russe. Ce fut l’un des grands mystères du début de la guerre en Ukraine. Habib Glenza , à Lödz Au début, des accusations ont été portées contre la Russie, mais très vite, le soupçon s’est tourbé vers l’Ukraine qui avait tiré profit de l’attaque contre le Nord Stream et qui pouvait être, de ce fait, à l’origine de cette opération. Les autorités allemandes ont mené l’enquête et ont remonté la piste jusqu’à Kuznetsov, un soldat ukrainien stationné en Italie. Son extradition a été demandée, il a été arrêté et est actuellement jugé en Allemagne. Kuznetsov a comparu pour la première fois devant le tribunal allemand, le mercredi 14 octobre 2026, faisant preuve d’un calme olympien. Il a même souri à plusieurs reprises. De graves accusations contre l’Ukraine Kuznetsov nie catégoriquement toute implication dans l’attaque contre le Nord Stream. L’Ukraine nie également tout lien avec le sabotage du gazoduc. Nicola Canestrini, l’avocat de la défense, a déclaré à la BBC que l’accusation ne reposait sur aucune preuve : «Ils n’ont trouvé aucun témoin, aucune preuve médico-légale, pas d’ADN, pas d’empreintes digitales, rien !» Comme si un agent des forces spéciales pouvait laisser ce genre d'indices lors de ses missions secrètes ! La défense a également fait valoir que Kuznetsov se trouve dans une position de faiblesse, puisqu’il est un soldat affecté à des opérations secrètes et ne peut pas parler de ce qu’il a fait aux dates auxquelles il est accusé d’avoir attaqué le Nord Stream. Argument très commode pour éviter de répondre aux questions des juges ! Un autre suspect impliqué dans l’attaque du Nord Stream se trouve en Croatie et lutte pour éviter son extradition vers l’Allemagne. Deux hypothèses sont avancées. La première suggère une implication des États-Unis dans les attaques contre le Nord Stream. Le journaliste chevronné Seymour Hersh (lauréat du prix Pulitzer pour avoir révélé des crimes commis par l’armée américaine, comme le massacre de Mỹ Lai au Vietnam) a publié un rapport faisant état de l’implication directe de plongeurs de la marine américaine. Ce rapport a été réfuté et contesté par d’autres journalistes, qui ont souligné les incohérences des preuves présentées. La seconde, avancée par des analystes et des journalistes spécialisés, suggère une hypothèse plus réaliste : la CIA était au courant du sabotage avant qu’il ait lieu, mais a décidé de le laisser se produire. L’attaque contre le Nord Stream aurait eu pour but de démontrer à l’Europe et à l’Allemagne en particulier que la guerre en Ukraine avait des conséquences directes sur son territoire. Il s’agissait d’un moyen de contraindre l’Union européenne à s’impliquer davantage dans la guerre et à soutenir Zelensky. ‘‘Le piège de Nord Stream’’ : De l’eau dans le gaz russe ? L’Europe et l’illusoire puissance Le procès des ambiguïtés occidentales Ce procès est délicat pour l’Ukraine comme pour l’Allemagne. Toutes deux sont alliées contre la Russie. Mais la justice allemande ne peut ignorer ce qui a porté un coup dur à une infrastructure vitale pour l’économie du pays. Par ailleurs, ce procès soulève un autre débat : est-il acceptable que l’Ukraine et la Russie bombardent des cibles non militaires telles que des infrastructures énergétiques, des centres de données ou des installations logistiques ? Ces attaques constituent-elles des crimes de guerre ? Poutine et Zelensky devraient-ils tous deux être jugés pour les avoir commis ? Cette affaire est un sujet épineux pour les puissances occidentales. S’il s’agit d’un sabotage perpétré par l’Ukraine, c’est une grave erreur, mais l’Ukraine est un pays ami qu’il faut protéger. Que faire ? Noyer le poisson ? C’est peut-être cette hypothèse qui fait sourire Kuznetsov, très à l’aise lors de son procès qui devrait se terminer en février 2027. En conclusion, la position occidentale concernant la guerre russo-ukrainienne alterne le clair et l’obscur, le chaud et le froid, et enveloppe d’un voile d’ambiguïté des motivations des différents protagonistes, notamment l’Ukraine, la Russie et l’Allemagne qui en ont été les plus affectés jusque-là. L’article Deux soldats ukrainiens auraient saboté les gazoducs Nord Stream 1 et 2 est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: Iran prolongs talks in stalemate to influence US midterms, officials say
items.description: By Parisa Hafezi DUBAI, Oct 20 (Reuters) - Iran has deliberately prolonged talks with the US to try to weaken Donald Trump politically ahead of November's US midterm elections, senior officials say, while fears of renewed military action and deep distrust of Washington have reinforced Tehran's reluctance to strike a quick deal to end the war. Three senior Iranian officials and an Iranian insider, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Tehran was convinced the US president was ready to resort to renewed attacks to try to break the stalemate in the eight-month-old war.

items.title: PPA board chair, deputy CEO and GIPS vice president honoured at 2026 ASCON Conference Awards
items.description: The Board Chairman of the Public Procurement Authority (PPA), Mr. Basil Ahiable, and two other astute procurement professionals, Rev. Celestine Djane and Dr. Ekow Ghansah, have earned recognition at the 2026 African Supply Chain Confederation (ASCON) Conference Awards, highlighting Ghana’s contribution to advancing procurement and supply chain management across the continent. Mr. Basil Ahiable was awarded as the SCM Governance Champion of the Year: Public Trust and Integrity Award, acknowledging his association with efforts to promote sound governance, transparency and integrity in procurement and supply chain management in his home country and across Africa. The recognition celebrates his commitment to public trust and ethical conduct in the management of procurement processes, particularly in ensuring accountability, responsible use of resources and value for money in both public and private sector operations. Rev. Celestine Djane—who is also the vice president of the Ghana Institute of Procurement and Supply (GIPS)—was named a finalist for the SCM Professional of the Year: Across the Continent Award, placing her among professionals whose wealth of experience has contributed immensely to the development of the supply chain management profession across the continent. Her nomination reflected the significance of professional expertise, continuous development and commitment to industry standards in strengthening procurement and supply chain practices across different economies on the continent. The third honoree, Dr. Ekow Ghansah, was also named a finalist in the SCM Executive of the Year Award category, which spotlighted leadership and executive contributions within the supply chain management profession. Dr. Ghansah’s nomination as a finalist showcased his executive leadership in driving organizational performance, improving procurement outcomes and building resilient supply chains that can respond to changing economic and business conditions. The recognition of the three astute procurement practitioners at the continental stage provides a platform highlights Ghana’s depth of expertise and participation in the advancement of procurement and supply chain management in Africa. The ASCON Awards form part of broader efforts by continent-wide procurement confederation to celebrate individuals and institutions contributing to the growth, professionalism and effectiveness of Africa’s supply chain sector. Such recognitions seek to encourage the adoption of sound governance practices, stronger professional standards and effective leadership across the industry. The president of the Ghana Institute of Procurement and Supply (GIPS), Dr. Simon Annan in a congratulatory, note has applauded the distinguished fellows of the Institute on their respective awards and finalist positions. According to him, the recognitions demonstrate the range of professional responsibilities represented within the institute’s leadership. “This recognition comes amid continuing efforts to strengthen procurement governance improve public expenditure management and promote professionalism in supply chain operations. These priorities are central to ensuring that procurement delivers measurable value and supports sustainable economic development,” he said.

items.title: CEDEAO–AES : des groupes de travail pour préparer un accord-cadre
items.description: © Internet Réunies à Dakar le 17 octobre, les deux organisations ont décidé d’engager des discussions techniques au sein de groupes de travail conjoints. Leurs conclusions seront examinées par les ministres avant une nouvelle session. La Communauté économique des États de l’Afrique de l’Ouest et la Confédération des États du Sahel ont tenu, samedi 17 octobre à Dakar, leur première session ministérielle consacrée à la coopération entre les deux organisations. La délégation de la CEDEAO était conduite par le ministre sénégalais des Affaires étrangères, Cheikh Niang, président du Conseil des ministres de l’organisation. Celle de l’AES était dirigée par son homologue burkinabè, Karamoko Jean-Marie Traoré, président du Comité ministériel de pilotage de la Confédération. Le Mali était représenté dans la délégation confédérale avec le Burkina Faso et le Niger. La réunion faisait suite aux consultations organisées le 22 mai 2025 à Bamako. Un mécanisme technique avant le prochain rendez-vous Le principal résultat consigné dans le communiqué conjoint concerne la création de groupes de travail thématiques. Ces groupes mèneront les discussions techniques destinées à préparer un accord-cadre de coopération entre la CEDEAO et l’AES. Leurs conclusions seront soumises aux ministres avant la prochaine session. La date, le lieu et la composition des groupes seront arrêtés par voie diplomatique. Le communiqué ne détaille pas encore les thèmes confiés à chaque groupe. Il fixe cependant les principes annoncés pour la suite des échanges : bon voisinage, respect de la souveraineté, dignité des États et protection des intérêts des populations. La rencontre de Dakar a donc établi une méthode de négociation. Elle n’a débouché ni sur un accord-cadre signé ni sur une modification immédiate des règles appliquées aux frontières. Les règles provisoires restent en vigueur Le Mali, le Burkina Faso et le Niger ont officiellement quitté la CEDEAO le 29 janvier 2025. Le même jour, l’organisation régionale avait adopté des dispositions transitoires pour limiter les perturbations touchant les citoyens et les activités économiques. La CEDEAO avait demandé à ses États membres de continuer à reconnaître les passeports et cartes d’identité portant son logo et détenus par les citoyens des trois pays. Elle avait aussi maintenu, jusqu’à nouvel ordre, la circulation, la résidence et l’établissement sans visa. Les biens et services provenant du Mali, du Burkina Faso et du Niger continuaient également à bénéficier du traitement prévu par le Schéma de libéralisation des échanges de la CEDEAO et sa politique d’investissement. Ces mesures devaient rester applicables jusqu’à la définition complète des nouvelles relations avec les trois États. L’accord-cadre annoncé à Dakar doit donner une base négociée à cette coopération entre deux organisations désormais distinctes. Pour les voyageurs, transporteurs et commerçants maliens, le régime en vigueur reste celui des dispositions transitoires de janvier 2025, dans l’attente des décisions issues des groupes de travail. Massiré Diop

items.title: Guinée : prolifération illégale des Web TV jusque dans les villages, la HAC menace de sanctions
items.description: La Haute Autorité de la Communication (HAC) annonce la fin de ses missions de sensibilisation sur les conditions légales de création des médias en République de Guinée, menées par ses commissaires dans toutes les préfectures du pays. Tout en remerciant les autorités et les acteurs des médias pour leur soutien, l’institution dénonce la prolifération des Web TV illégales et prévient qu’elle se réserve le droit de sanctionner les contrevenants. Dans un communiqué signé de son Président Boubacar Yacine Diallo, la HAC tient à exprimer sa « profonde gratitude et ses remerciements les plus sincères » aux autorités administratives, judiciaires et religieuses, ainsi qu’aux acteurs des médias qui ont accordé « un intérêt particulier et un soutien constant » à ces missions de vulgarisation de la réglementation. Cependant, l’institution déplore la poursuite de la prolifération des Web TV illégales, malgré cette campagne de sensibilisation et d’explication des textes légaux. « Cependant, l’institution regrette fermement de constater que, malgré cette campagne de sensibilisation et d’explication des textes légaux, la prolifération de Web TV illégales se poursuit, s’étendant désormais jusqu’à nos villages », souligne le communiqué. La HAC dénonce des installations réalisées en violation des procédures d’autorisation, ainsi que le recours à du personnel non professionnel, estimant que ces pratiques compromettent gravement l’éthique et la déontologie journalistiques. Elle rappelle que « la création et l’exploitation de tout média en Guinée sont soumises au respect strict du cadre juridique en vigueur ». Face à cette situation, l’institution hausse le ton et annonce des mesures contre les contrevenants. « En conséquence, à compter de la date de publication du présent communiqué, la HAC se réserve le droit de sanctionner avec la plus grande rigueur tous les manquements constatés », prévient-elle. Enfin, la HAC invite l’ensemble des promoteurs et acteurs des médias à se conformer sans délai aux lois de la République afin de garantir un paysage médiatique libre, responsable et professionnel. « La HAC invite l’ensemble des promoteurs et acteurs des médias à se conformer sans délai aux lois de la République afin de garantir un paysage médiatique libre, responsable et Professionnel », conclut le communiqué. items.title: Black Queens drop five places in Fifa global ranking, drop to fifth in Africa
items.description: The Black Queens have fallen in the latest FIFA Women’s World Rankings, dropping five places in the list revealed on Tuesday, October 20. The latest ranking shows Ghana dropping to 65th place globally from their previous 60th position. The ranking is based on the team’s performance at the 2026 Women’s Africa Cup of Nations (WAFCON) tournament, which was staged in Morocco in July and August. The Black Queens were knocked out of the competition in the quarterfinals by Malawi and failed to make the semifinals of the competition, missing out on an automatic slot to the 2027 Women’s World Cup. Ghana also faced Mauritius as part of the qualification phase for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic Games. The result of the ranking shows a concern, having seen Ghana rise to 60th in the previous outcome. On the continent, Ghana has also lost its third-place slot and dropped to the fifth on the ranking. its third-place South Africa and Morocco have moved above the Black Queens, while Nigeria continues to stay at the top of the ranking. The Black Queens are expected in action next month when they play in the preliminary phase of the playoff tournament for the 2027 Women’s World Cup.

items.title: ‘He let Manchester United down’ – Ten Hag recounts fallout with Ronaldo
items.description: Former Manchester United manager Erik ten Hag has accused Cristiano Ronaldo of letting both the club and him down during their time together at Old Trafford, alleging that the Portuguese forward failed to meet the team’s fitness and training standards. Ten Hag made the remarks in an exclusive interview with The Athletic on Tuesday, reflecting on his difficult relationship with the five-time Ballon d’Or winner during his tenure as United manager. “He let the team down, and he let me down, because we planned with him,” Ten Hag said. “I flew out to Portugal to speak with him about what I was aiming for before I came to United.” Despite his criticism, the Dutchman acknowledged Ronaldo’s place in football history, describing him as one of the game’s greatest players. “Obviously, he’s one of the best in football history. I respected him a lot. But at that time, as a manager, I had to make a rational decision,” he added. Ten Hag also alleged that Ronaldo struggled to meet the club’s fitness requirements, claiming that the forward sometimes withdrew from training sessions and failed to achieve the required heart rate levels. He also recalled an incident after United’s 4-0 defeat to Brentford in August 2022, when players had to run laps as punishment. According to Ten Hag, Ronaldo completed only two of the three laps. The former manager said he confronted Ronaldo over his fitness and positioning, insisting that the forward needed to work harder to put himself in scoring positions. “I confronted him with this,” Ten Hag said. “Many times I say, ‘Ronnie, everyone wants to work for you to bring you in the right position, but if you can’t bring yourself in the box, you can’t score’. He was not capable to do this.” Ten Hag also claimed that Ronaldo did not contribute sufficiently to the team’s pressing and defensive work, alleging that the forward encouraged teammates to conserve their energy during training. “Ronaldo was telling the players: save your legs at training,” he said. “I understand it when you are top fit, but first you have to train yourself to get into the right fitness levels.” The Dutchman maintained that while managers must accommodate their best players, star footballers must also accept their responsibilities to the team. “Every top team has to embrace the top player, but the top player has to work for the team,” Ten Hag said. Ronaldo’s relationship with Ten Hag deteriorated during the 2022/23 season, culminating in the forward’s departure from Manchester United in November 2022 following a controversial interview in which he criticised the club and its management. The post ‘He let Manchester United down’ – Ten Hag recounts fallout with Ronaldo appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: États-Unis : une campagne à l’étude pour attirer davantage d’Afrikaners comme réfugiés
items.description: L'administration Trump cherche a relancer les candidatures des Afrikaners, apres un ralentissement des demandes. Selon The Guardian , le departement d'etat americain examine une campagne de communication de 335 000 dollars en Afrique du Sud, avec un sondage, des groupes de discussion et de la publicite numerique en afrikaans. L'objectif est de comprendre pourquoi les Sud-Africains blancs sont moins nombreux que prevu a solliciter le statut de refugie et d'encourager de nouvelles demandes. La mesure remonte a 2025, lorsque le president americain Donald Trump a decide de donner la priorite aux Afrikaners, qu'il presente comme victimes de discriminations, de violences et de menaces sur leurs terres. Pretoria conteste ce discours et rejette l'idee d'une persecution systematique des Sud-Africains blancs. Elle estime que le nombre relativement faible de demandes fragilise l'argument americain selon lequel les Afrikaners chercheraient massivement a fuir le pays. Un plafond de 17 500 admissions pour 2027 Malgre ce ralentissement, le dispositif reste tres favorable aux Afrikaners. Au cours de l'exercice 2026, les etats-Unis ont admis 16 292 refugies, presque tous sud-africains. Pour 2027, l'administration a fixe un plafond de 17 500 admissions, qui doivent a nouveau beneficier principalement aux Afrikaners. Le coût de leur reinstallation est estime a 500 millions de dollars. Cet accueil prioritaire contraste fortement avec le durcissement general de l'immigration sous Trump. L'administration a reduit les admissions de refugies venus d'autres regions et reexamine des milliers de dossiers herites de l'ere Biden. Les associations de defense des refugies denoncent une selection fondee sur des criteres politiques et raciaux.

items.title: Energy Ministry woos investors as PHDC signs Global Sphere deal for Petroleum Hub Phase Two
items.description: The Minister of Energy and Green Transition, Dr John Jinapor, has reaffirmed government’s commitment to creating a credible, competitive and investor-friendly energy sector to attract investment and support sustainable growth. “As a government, we are committed to building a credible, competitive and investor-friendly energy sector anchored on certainty, predictability and transparency,” Dr Jinapor said in a Facebook post following bilateral meetings with key industry players on the sidelines of African Energy Week. The meetings brought together companies already operating in Ghana and prospective investors interested in exploring opportunities in the country’s energy sector. The companies commended Ghana for the economic turnaround achieved within a year and the government’s efforts to make the energy sector more attractive to investors. “These principles are cardinal to strengthening investor confidence, fostering long-term partnerships and creating an enabling environment for sustainable investment and growth in the energy sector,” he added. In a related development, Dr Jinapor witnessed the signing of a partnership agreement between the Petroleum Hub Development Corporation (PHDC) and Global Sphere for Phase Two of the Petroleum Hub Project. He described the partnership as a significant milestone in Ghana’s ambition to become West Africa’s leading energy hub. The minister said the project would help drive industrialisation, attract investment, create jobs and strengthen the country’s energy security. The project, scheduled for development over five years, will comprise a refinery with a capacity of 300,000 barrels per stream day, two petrochemical plants, storage facilities with a combined capacity of four million cubic metres and a multi-berth jetty. Dr Jinapor commended all stakeholders for their commitment to the project and pledged to work closely with the PHDC to fulfil the government’s obligations and move the initiative from agreements to actual construction. “You have my full support. I will engage the Minister of Finance and the Attorney-General. I will also bring on board the Minister of Lands and Natural Resources so that, together, we can guide this project and provide the necessary backing,” he said. He also commended the PHDC, led by its Chief Executive Officer, Dr Toni Aubynn, for its efforts to advance the initiative, stressing the need for full institutional support to deliver a project central to President John Dramani Mahama’s ambitions for Ghana’s oil and gas sector. Dr Aubynn described Dr Jinapor as a consistent supporter of the petroleum hub initiative and said the corporation had made implementation a priority in 2026. He said the project was intended to become a strategic national asset that would strengthen energy security, create jobs and reduce Ghana’s exposure to external economic shocks, including geopolitical tensions affecting global energy markets. “We believed that the groundwork had been laid, that the partnerships were within our reach, and that the time had come to move from boardroom plans on paper to progress on the ground,” he said.

items.title: Le Petit Séminaire Saint-Luc célèbre ses 50 ans
items.description: Le Petit Séminaire Saint-Luc de Saint-Louis a célébré son jubilé d’or, marquant cinq décennies de formation et de promotion des vocations sacerdotales. Cet anniversaire a coïncidé avec l’installation de son nouveau directeur, l’abbé Louis Gomis, et celle de l’abbé Nzaly Gragini Kaly comme curé de la paroisse Notre-Dame-de-Lourdes. Une double célébration placée sous le signe de l’action de grâce, de l’engagement et de la solidarité. La cérémonie a été présidée par l’évêque de Saint-Louis Mgr Augustin Simmel Ndiaye en présence du préfet du département de Saint-Louis. Cinquante ans au service de l’Église et de la société. Le Petit Séminaire Saint-Luc de Saint-Louis a célébré son jubilé d’or dans un esprit de reconnaissance envers Dieu et de renouvellement de sa mission. Pour l’abbé André Nalla Mandef, directeur sortant et responsable de l’organisation, cet anniversaire constitue une étape importante. « Vivre 50 ans pour une structure n’est pas du tout une chose facile. C’est surtout rendre grâce à Dieu, parce que c’est lui qui nous a permis de vivre ces 50 ans », a-t-il déclaré. Après cinq années à la tête de l’établissement, désormais nommé curé de la paroisse des Martyrs de l’Ouganda de Matam, il a appelé les fidèles à soutenir davantage le séminaire. « C’est la pépinière, c’est là où l’évêque sème », a-t-il rappelé, invitant les Saint-Louisiens à contribuer régulièrement à la prise en charge des séminaristes. Nommé nouveau directeur, l’abbé Louis Gomis a rappelé que le séminaire a été lancé le 18 octobre 1976 par Mgr Pierre Sagna, avec pour objectif de promouvoir les vocations et de former un clergé local. Depuis cinq décennies, l’établissement accompagne les jeunes dans leur discernement et leur préparation à la vie sacerdotale. « Le prêtre est un ministre de l’Église, mais aussi un ministre chargé du service pour le bien-être de toute la population », a-t-il souligné. Notre-Dame-de-Lourdes : un appel à l’engagement Il a également insisté sur le rôle des familles chrétiennes dans l’éveil des vocations et sur l’importance d’une formation humaine, intellectuelle et spirituelle adaptée aux défis contemporains. La cérémonie a également été marquée par l’installation de l’abbé Nzaly Gragini Kaly comme nouveau curé de la paroisse Notre-Dame-de-Lourdes par Mgr Augustin Simmel Ndiaye évêque du diocèse de Saint-Louis. Désormais en fonction, il entend promouvoir la collaboration avec les fidèles pour relever les défis de la communauté paroissiale. Il a notamment évoqué la nécessité de rénover l’église et la maison des prêtres, appelant les paroissiens, les bienfaiteurs et les personnes de bonne volonté à contribuer à ces projets. « C’est main dans la main, dans la synodalité, que nous pourrons aller de l’avant », a-t-il affirmé, plaidant pour une mobilisation collective. À travers ces deux événements, l’Église locale réaffirme ainsi son engagement en faveur de la formation, de la transmission de la foi et du service communautaire. Jeanne SAGNA (Correspondante)

items.title: China opposes US ban on govt agencies from using DeepSeek
items.description: Beijing opposed on Tuesday a US government ban on its agencies using AI tools from Chinese startup DeepSeek, saying the move “overstretched” the concept of national security. China and the United States are locked in a race for dominance in the fast-moving artificial intelligence sector, trading accusations of stealing AI technologies and jeopardising security in recent months. The US Department of Homeland Security on Monday banned products developed by DeepSeek — and tools created using DeepSeek by third parties — saying they risked sharing sensitive data with China. Beijing’s foreign ministry opposed the ban on Tuesday, vowing to protect Chinese businesses. “China has consistently opposed the overstretching of the concept of national security and the politicisation of issues related to science, technology, and trade,” ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told a news conference. The Department of Homeland Security can issue directions to civilian agencies, but not the military or intelligence services. Its statement on Monday said that “DeepSeek’s models multiple threat vectors” and must be removed from IT devices. Use of DeepSeek AI tools “may result in the transfer of sensitive data to (China) if used by US government employees or vendors,” the department warned. Its servers are located in China, where the legal system permits the government “extensive authority” to access private company infrastructure, it said. AFP has contacted DeepSeek for comment. DeepSeek, one of China’s top AI labs, shook up the industry in January 2025 with a low-cost, high-performance chatbot, challenging assumptions of US dominance. The firm released a long-awaited new model, V4, in April and this month updated a faster, more lightweight version of V4. The United States has accused DeepSeek and other top Chinese AI firms of systematically stealing the capabilities of cutting-edge models developed by American rivals. Despite their fierce competition in the field, China and the United States in September agreed to set up a “communication channel” for AI incidents. The topic is expected to arise again when the countries’ leaders meet next month at a summit in the Chinese city of Shenzhen. items.title: Kome Shime Traditional Council inducts six new chiefs and queen mothers in Whuti
items.description: The Kome Shime Traditional Council has inducted six new members following a swearing-in ceremony held at Whuti in the Volta Region on Wednesday, October 14, 2026. The ceremony formally welcomed the traditional leaders into the Council, with officials saying the move would strengthen its representation and support traditional governance within the Kome Shime Traditional Area and Anlo State. The newly inducted members are Togbi Agbelom Agbotokor Dzreke II, Divisional Chief of Salo-Sokutsime; Togbi Tsikata Agbodzie II, Divisional Chief of Srogboe; and Mama Amedzor II, Divisional Queenmother of Salo-Sokutsime. The others are Togbi Lagah Doe Dzata V, Sub-Divisional Chief of Whuti; Mama Agume Dzonu II, Sub-Divisional Queenmother of Whuti; and Mama Kordeku II, Sub-Divisional Queenmother of Srogboe. During the ceremony, the six members swore the Oath of Secrecy, Judicial Oath and Oath of Membership. The oaths were administered by Her Honour Bridget Akpe Akattah, Judge in charge of the Keta Circuit Court. The Registrar of the Kome Shime Traditional Council, Kafui Logoh, reminded the new members that the oaths carried obligations that must guide their conduct and decisions in the discharge of their duties. The Paramount Chief and President of the Council, Togbi Nyaho Tamakloe VI, congratulated the leaders on their induction and urged them to perform their responsibilities with integrity, fairness and a strong sense of duty. He stressed the need for high ethical standards and encouraged the traditional leaders to pursue amicable and peaceful resolutions to chieftaincy disputes. Togbi Nyaho Tamakloe VI also reiterated that although the Kome Shime Traditional Area and Council was autonomous under Legislative Instrument (L.I.) 2409, its members remained indigenes of Anlo and were expected to participate in Anlo customs and traditions when called upon. He urged the members to place the collective interests of Anlo Dukor and Ghana above personal interests, stressing that unity and collaboration among traditional authorities were essential to maintaining peace and supporting development. The induction marks another step in the Council’s efforts to strengthen traditional leadership and promote harmonious relations among communities within its jurisdiction.
