items.title: Mahama links rising foreign investment to improving economic stability
items.description: President John Dramani Mahama says improving economic stability is strengthening investor confidence in Ghana, with foreign direct investment (FDI) inflows rising to US$2.62 billion in 2025 from US$624 million in 2024. He disclosed this at the sod-cutting ceremony for the 1,238-acre Afienya Industrial Park, where he linked the increase in foreign investment to improving economic conditions and renewed interest in the country. President Mahama attributed the growth to declining inflation and interest rates, alongside greater stability in the local currency, which he said were helping to position Ghana as an attractive destination for long-term investment. “The stability of the Ghanaian economy is attracting strong interest from global investors,” he said, adding that the trend reflected growing confidence in the government’s leadership and its efforts to channel investment into viable sectors with significant economic potential. President Mahama also pointed to the Tema Export Processing Zone’s role in Ghana’s industrial growth over the past 30 years, saying its success offers valuable lessons for the development of future industrial parks. According to figures from the Ghana Free Zones Authority (GFZA), the Tema zone has supported more than 80 industrial enterprises and generated over US$24 billion in cumulative export revenue over 30 years. It also recorded US$3.1 billion in exports in 2025. A further US$1.4 billion in exports was recorded in the first half of 2026, putting the country on course to match or exceed the previous year’s performance if the trend continues. The zone has also sustained more than 78,000 direct jobs, with Ghanaians accounting for 98 per cent of the workforce. “Behind these figures are real households in Tema, Ashaiman, Shai Hills, and surrounding communities whose livelihoods depend on these opportunities,” President Mahama said. He stressed the need to build on the Tema zone’s experience by ensuring that new industrial hubs provide reliable services, strengthen links with local businesses and deliver lasting benefits to their host communities. Turning to the Afienya Industrial Park, the President assured prospective local and international investors that the development was being planned to address common operational challenges associated with setting up businesses. He said the 1,238-acre site was free from land litigation and would be equipped with essential infrastructure, including electricity, water, road access and digital connectivity, to facilitate the establishment of factories. “At Afienya, our goal is to translate industrial policy into tangible, practical opportunities for businesses and job seekers alike,” he said. President Mahama added that the industrial expansion formed part of the government’s flagship New Economy Policy, scheduled for implementation in 2027. The policy is expected to accelerate structural transformation, increase domestic value addition and strengthen Ghana’s position as an export hub within the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA).

items.title: Cinq ans après, Rufisque se souvient d’une figure emblématique
items.description: Ancien maire de Rufisque, député, sénateur et président de l’ASC Les Saltigués, Mamadou Cora Fall est décédé le 20 octobre 2021, à l’âge de 83 ans. Cinq ans après sa disparition, son parcours reste associé à la vie politique, sociale et sportive de la vieille ville. Il était de ces hommes dont le nom reste étroitement lié à l’histoire de leur ville. Mamadou Cora Fall, ancien maire de Rufisque, s’est éteint dans la nuit du 19 au 20 octobre 2021, à l’âge de 83 ans. Cinq ans après sa disparition, son souvenir demeure présent dans une ville où il a exercé des responsabilités politiques et consacré une grande partie de sa vie au mouvement sportif. Né le 14 mars 1938 à Rufisque, Mamadou Cora Fall a connu une longue carrière politique. Selon les informations publiées par la presse sénégalaise au lendemain de son décès, il a été maire de Rufisque de 1984 à 1987. Il a ensuite occupé d’autres fonctions électives, notamment celles de député et de sénateur. Il a également dirigé la commune de Rufisque-Ouest et exercé des responsabilités au sein de la communauté urbaine de Dakar. Son parcours a été marqué par les évolutions et les rivalités de la vie politique locale. Figure connue de la scène politique rufisquoise, il a notamment évolué au sein du Parti socialiste avant de rejoindre, plus tard, le Parti démocratique sénégalais. Son itinéraire témoigne des recompositions politiques qui ont marqué la vie publique sénégalaise au fil des décennies. Un engagement au-delà de la politique Mais réduire Mamadou Cora Fall à ses fonctions politiques serait incomplet. À Rufisque, son nom est également associé au sport. Il a présidé pendant plusieurs décennies l’ASC Les Saltigués, l’un des clubs emblématiques de la ville, engagé dans plusieurs disciplines sportives. Sous sa présidence, le club a notamment connu un moment important avec sa victoire en Coupe du Sénégal de football en 1977 face au Dial Diop de Dakar. Cet épisode reste l’un des repères du parcours sportif des Saltigués et de leur histoire dans le football sénégalais. Sa présence durable à la tête du club a fait de lui un acteur important du mouvement sportif local. Au-delà du football, les Saltigués étaient engagés dans d’autres disciplines, notamment le basketball, le handball, le volleyball et l’athlétisme. Son investissement dans cette structure a contribué à renforcer son ancrage dans la vie de la cité. Figure du paysage rufisquois Mamadou Cora Fall était également connu pour son implication dans les questions sociales. Cette proximité avec les populations a participé à l’image d’un responsable politique dont l’influence dépassait les institutions. Son engagement local, conjugué à ses responsabilités électives et sportives, lui a permis de conserver une place particulière dans la mémoire de nombreux Rufisquois. Sa disparition avait suscité des réactions dans les milieux politiques et sportifs. Le ministre des Sports de l’époque, Matar Bâ, avait notamment salué la mémoire d’un homme qui avait, selon ses termes, « toujours donné le bon exemple et accompli son devoir, sa vie durant ». Mamadou Cora Fall a été inhumé au cimetière musulman de Diokoul, à Rufisque-Ouest. Il laisse derrière lui le souvenir d’un homme engagé dans plusieurs domaines de la vie publique, dont le parcours s’est construit au contact de sa ville.

items.title: Le Sénégal lance sa taxonomie verte
items.description: Le Sénégal s’est doté, lundi 19 octobre 2026, d’une taxonomie (système de classification) verte. L’adoption de cet outil vise à faciliter l’identification, la compréhension et la conformité des projets stratégiques aux exigences environnementales. Cette politique de durabilité vient renforcer la confiance des investisseurs et des partenaires internationaux. L’adaptation aux changements climatiques invite à un changement de paradigmes dans la manière de financer les projets à fort impact socioéconomique. Désormais, les gouvernants doivent inscrire la durabilité au cœur de leurs actions pour renforcer la confiance des investisseurs et des partenaires au développement. C’est dans cette logique que le Sénégal, engagé dans une politique de transition écologique, a adopté, hier, lundi 19 octobre, une taxonomie verte. Cette stratégie de classification du degré de durabilité des projets est portée par le ministère de l’Environnement et celui chargé de l’Économie, des Finances et du Plan, avec l’appui technique de la Coopération allemande (Giz). La taxonomie verte vise à renforcer l’atténuation des effets du changement climatique dans les secteurs de l’industrie, des transports, de l’énergie, de la construction, de l’eau, de l’assainissement et de l’agriculture. Cet engagement en faveur de la cause environnementale traduit la volonté du Sénégal à contribuer fortement à la mise en œuvre des réformes structurantes du secteur financier. Selon le ministre de l’Environnement et de la Transition écologique, Aliou Gori Diouf, le développement économique et la protection de l’environnement ne s’opposent pas, ils avancent ensemble. « Nous voulons une économie qui crée de la richesse en préservant ses ressources, qui crée des emplois en renforçant sa résilience, qui attire les investissements en respectant la durabilité. Avec cette taxonomie, nous passons de l’ambition à l’action et de l’engagement à l’investissement concret », a-t-il souligné. Un besoin évalué à plus de 7.500 milliards de FCfa Ce nouvel outil, adopté par le Sénégal, vient renforcer le dispositif existant et inscrire le pays sur la liste des économies qui tiennent compte des défis environnementaux. « Ces investissements ne sont pas seulement une réponse aux changements climatiques, ils peuvent renforcer la compétitivité, développer de nouvelles filières économiques et créer des emplois durables », a précisé Kai Baldow, ambassadeur de la République fédérale d’Allemagne au Sénégal. La mise en œuvre de cette ambitieuse politique de taxonomie verte nécessitera néanmoins la mobilisation de capitaux considérables. D’où l’urgence de disposer de ressources supplémentaires afin de réussir le pari de la transition écologique. « Cette dynamique doit reposer sur l’appropriation de l’outil par les acteurs clés de l’écosystème financier, un dialogue et une coopération renforcés, ainsi que notre volonté partagée de faire progresser notre pays vers une économie plus verte, plus résiliente, plus inclusive et plus durable », a invité le ministre chargé du Budget, Bassirou Sarr. La taxonomie contribue à une économie durable, oriente les capitaux et donne aux investisseurs, aux banques et aux entreprises la visibilité dont ils ont besoin pour agir. Elle participe à la réduction du risque de « greenwhasing » tout en renforçant la transparence des marchés. Avec la classification des activités économiques, le Sénégal s’engage dans une dynamique d’atténuation du changement climatique, d’adaptation et de résilience. La Contribution déterminée au niveau national (Cdn) a besoin de 13 milliards de dollars (7.595 milliards FCfa) pour dérouler la vision des autorités publiques d’ici à 2030. « Évaluée à 13 milliards de dollars, notre Contribution déterminée au niveau national intègre 8,2 milliards de dollars (soit 4.791 milliards de FCfa) de financements conditionnels pour couvrir les besoins du Sénégal à l’horizon 2030. Aucun budget public, aucune aide extérieure ne suffira seule à les couvrir. Il faut convaincre les capitaux privés, et pour les convaincre, il faut leur parler clairement », a expliqué le Dr Aliou Gori Diouf. Ce besoin nécessite, au-delà des efforts internes, une mobilisation des acteurs publics et privés pour porter cette ambition. Diégane DIOUF

items.title: Escroquerie présumée : un crédit-bail de 10 véhicules au cœur d’une affaire de 231,9 millions de FCFA
items.description: La Division des investigations criminelles (DIC) a déféré, le 19 octobre 2026, au parquet de Dakar un individu poursuivi pour une escroquerie présumée portant sur un préjudice de 231,9 millions de FCFA. Le mis en cause aurait obtenu un crédit-bail portant sur 10 véhicules avant de cesser les remboursements, après le paiement d’une seule mensualité. Des faux relevés bancaires auraient également été utilisés pour monter le dossier. Selon les informations communiquées par la Police nationale, l’affaire a débuté lorsqu’une banque a accordé au mis en cause un crédit-bail portant sur 10 véhicules, avec des mensualités de 3,9 millions de FCFA sur une durée de 60 mois, soit un montant total de 234 millions de FCFA. Après s’être acquitté de la première échéance, l’intéressé serait devenu injoignable, tout en continuant à exploiter les véhicules. L’examen de son dossier de financement aurait par ailleurs révélé que les relevés bancaires fournis étaient de faux documents. Convoqué à plusieurs reprises, il aurait refusé de répondre aux convocations des enquêteurs et de restituer les véhicules. Interpellé par la suite, il a reconnu n’avoir payé que la première mensualité, imputant le défaut de paiement à ses partenaires, qui n’auraient pas honoré leurs engagements financiers. Confronté aux incohérences relevées dans son dossier, le mis en cause a également fini par reconnaître avoir confectionné lui-même les faux relevés bancaires. Les enquêteurs ont pu localiser les véhicules grâce à leurs balises GPS, avant de procéder à leur immobilisation. Selon la Police nationale, l’individu est un récidiviste, déjà condamné pour des faits similaires en novembre 2025. Le dossier a été transmis au parquet de Dakar, qui devra donner les suites judiciaires appropriées à cette affaire. A.N

items.title: Bourse de Casablanca : ouverture en hausse
items.description: La Bourse de Casablanca a démarré en hausse mardi, son indice phare, le MASI, progressant de 0,08% à 16.988,99 points (pts). Le MASI 20, qui regroupe les 20 valeurs les plus liquides, augmentait de 0,17% à 1.228,38 pts et le MASI ESG, indice des entreprises ayant la meilleure notation ESG selon Moody's ESG Solutions, avançait de 0,16% à 1.255,26 pts. Le MASI Mid and Small Cap, qui reflète la performance des petites et moyennes capitalisations, prenait 0,02% à 1.619,13 pts. Aux valeurs individuelles, Colorado (+6,15% à 77,49 DH), Med Paper (+4,31% à 23 DH), HPS (+2,8% à 532,5 DH), Bank of Africa (+2,72% à 184,9 DH) et Involys (+1,72% à 118 DH) réalisaient les meilleures performances. Contre-tendance, les plus fortes baisses étaient accusées par Ib Maroc.com (-4,02% à 52 DH), SNEP (-2,2% à 277,7 DH), CMPG Group (-1,68% à 263 DH), AtlantaSanad (-1,63% à 118,05 DH) et Minière Touissit (-1,23% à 4.000 DH). La veille, le MASI avait clôturé sur une perte de 0,13%. The post Bourse de Casablanca : ouverture en hausse appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Menaces sur les oliveraies tunisiennes
items.description: La Tunisie prend des mesures pour contrer la propagation de la tuberculose de l’olivier, une maladie bactérienne qui menace cette culture importante pour l'économie du pays. Parallèlement, les prévisions pour la campagne oléicole 2026-2027 indiquent une baisse de la production d’environ 40 % par rapport à la saison précédente, qui pourrait être encore davantage impactée par la recrudescence de cette maladie. Le ministère de l’Agriculture a annoncé un programme exceptionnel d’interventions phytosanitaires, suite à la détection de foyers dans la zone de Melloulech, située dans le gouvernorat côtier de Mahdia — une région du pays à forte vocation oléicole. Cette maladie, également appelée «tuberculose de l’olivier» , est causée par la bactérie Pseudomonas savastano i. Elle se manifeste par des excroissances noueuses sur les branches et les troncs, susceptibles de compromettre la vitalité des arbres et de réduire leur productivité. L’agent pathogène se propage principalement par le biais de lésions de l’écorce, favorisées notamment par les opérations de taille et l’utilisation d’outils agricoles contaminés. Selon un communiqué du ministère de l’Agriculture, des équipes techniques pluridisciplinaires sont à pied d’œuvre dans les zones concernées depuis fin septembre, afin d’évaluer l’étendue des infections et d’identifier les arbres touchés. Le plan d’urgence prévoit le confinement des zones infectées, l’élagage des arbres les plus gravement atteints, l’élimination des résidus végétaux infectés par brûlage contrôlé, ainsi que des traitements préventifs dans les oliveraies avoisinantes. Surveillance dans tous les gouvernorats oléicoles Les autorités ont par ailleurs mis en place des équipes régionales de surveillance dans tous les gouvernorats oléicoles, chargées de détecter rapidement tout nouveau foyer d’infection. Aucune donnée officielle n’a encore été communiquée concernant les superficies touchées, ni aucune évaluation quantitative des pertes de production imputables à la maladie. Cette urgence phytosanitaire survient à une période délicate pour le secteur. Selon Najah Saïdi Hamed, présidente de la Chambre nationale des producteurs d’olives, la production tunisienne d’huile devrait s’établir autour de 300 000 tonnes pour la campagne 2026-2027, contre environ 500 000 tonnes estimées pour la campagne précédente, soit une baisse de 200 000 tonnes (40 %). Comment lutter contre la tuberculose de l’olivier signalée à Mahdia et Sfax Ce recul est principalement attribué au phénomène d’alternance biennale des oliviers : après une saison particulièrement abondante, les arbres ont tendance à enregistrer des rendements plus faibles. Par conséquent, il n’existe pas, à l’heure actuelle, d’éléments permettant d’établir un lien direct entre la baisse de production nationale prévue et la tuberculose de l’olivier. Toutefois, la prévision, formulée dès début septembre, a précédé l’annonce de l’urgence bactérienne. Les enjeux sont importants pour l’économie tunisienne. En 2025, les exportations d’huile d'olive ont généré environ 4,07 milliards de dinars, soit l’équivalent d’environ 1,35 milliard de dollars. Au cours des dix premiers mois de la campagne 2025-2026, de novembre à août, les ventes à l’étranger ont atteint 381 200 tonnes, pour une valeur de 4,78 milliards de dinars, selon les données de l’Observatoire national de l'agriculture (Onagri). L’Union européenne demeure la principale destination, absorbant 56,6 % des exportations en volume, tandis que l’Espagne et l’Italie en captent respectivement 31,9 % et 19,8 %. Environ 85,5 % de l’huile tunisienne exportée continue d’être commercialisée en vrac. Une récolte moins abondante pourrait avoir une incidence sur les quantités destinées à l’exportation ainsi que sur les prix ; toutefois, une éventuelle hausse des cours internationaux pourrait compenser, au moins partiellement, la baisse des volumes. I. B. L’article Menaces sur les oliveraies tunisiennes est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: Arturo Pérez-Reverte: “Me pone caliente cada nueva novela, cada batalla me obliga a ser joven de nuevo”
items.description: En la luminosa isla napolitana de Prócida, cuando desde el puerto llegas por una calle empinada a la bonita piazzetta Sèmmarèzio —actual plaza de los Mártires—, al lado de la iglesia de la Madonna della Grazie, se abre inesperadamente un panorama de no creérselo. Es el Mediterráneo todo el que se extiende hasta el infinito en una imprevista explosión de azul y de luz que llena el corazón de júbilo y de un extraño anhelo. Hay un hombre de espaldas contemplando ensimismado el mar desde la privilegiada atalaya del mirador. Su quietud y su porte lo hacen rivalizar con los de la estatua que preside la placita. Dado que el que observa las aguas con el conocimiento de causa de un Billy Bones es el escritor Arturo Pérez-Reverte la situación pide que el monumento sea de un marino ilustre, un navegante indómito o un capitán corsario; sin embargo se trata del insigne Antonio Scialoja, economista y político del Risorgimento, que no dejó de vivir aventuras: fue exiliado y volvió como ministro del primer gobierno de Garibaldi. items.title: Troops rescue 27 kidnapped victims in Katsina, recover motorcycles
items.description: By Kingsley Omonobi Troops of Operation Fansan Yamma have recorded another operational success with the rescue of 27 kidnapped victims and recovery of a motorcycle in Katsina State. Lieutenant Colonel Aliyu Danja, Media Information Officer, made this known on Tuesday, noting that the successful operations underscore the sustained offensive posture and operational effectiveness of troops of Operation Fansan Yamma. He said, “On 16 October 2026, troops of Sector 1 received a distress call on terrorist activities in Gamji community, Sabuwa Local Government Area. “It was reported that terrorists had abducted 27 residents, comprising 15 males and 12 females. “Troops responded swiftly, pursuing the terrorists along the Gangare–Kamba axis. “On contact, troops engaged with superior firepower, forcing the terrorists to abandon their victims and flee in disarray. “All 27 victims were rescued unharmed during exploitation of the area. “They have been profiled and handed over to community leaders for reunification with their families. “In a separate operation on the same day, troops conducting fighting patrol around Kurba village in Kankara Local Government Area encountered terrorists on 3 motorcycles. “The terrorists fled on sighting troops, abandoning one motorcycle. “The successful operations underscore the sustained offensive posture and operational effectiveness of troops of Operation Fansan Yamma in denying terrorists freedom of action and safeguarding vulnerable communities across the Joint Operations Area. “The Theatre Commander, Joint Task Force North West, Operation Fansan Yamma, commends troops for their gallantry and swift response. “He assures residents of Katsina, Zamfara and adjoining states of the Task Force’s unwavering commitment to restoring lasting peace and security.” The post Troops rescue 27 kidnapped victims in Katsina, recover motorcycles appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Energy Minister pledges inter-ministerial push to unblock Petroleum Hub project
items.description: The Minister for Energy and Green Transition, Dr John Abdulai Jinapor, has pledged to lead inter-ministerial engagements to resolve outstanding land acquisition, compensation and financing issues delaying the development of Ghana’s Petroleum Hub. Dr Jinapor said he would engage the Ministries of Finance and Lands and Natural Resources, as well as the Attorney-General’s Office, to address the challenges and create the conditions necessary for the project to progress. His commitment follows the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between the Petroleum Hub Development Corporation (PHDC) and an investment consortium led by Global Sphere of the United Arab Emirates for the development of Lot 2 of the project. Speaking at the signing ceremony, Dr Jinapor said the interest demonstrated by investors must be matched by decisive action from government institutions to remove obstacles to implementation. “You have my full support. I will engage the Minister of Finance and the Attorney-General. I will also bring on board the Minister of Lands and Natural Resources so that, together, we can guide this project and provide the necessary backing,” he said. The minister pledged to work closely with the PHDC to fulfil the government’s obligations and ensure the project moves beyond agreements to actual construction. He also commended the Corporation, led by its Chief Executive Officer, Dr Toni Aubynn, for its efforts to advance the initiative, stressing the need for full institutional support to deliver a project central to President John Dramani Mahama’s ambitions for Ghana’s oil and gas sector. Dr Aubynn described Dr Jinapor as a consistent supporter of the Petroleum Hub and said the Corporation had made implementation a priority in 2026. The proposed Petroleum Hub is intended to advance Ghana’s position in the regional petroleum industry, with the development of Lot 2 marking another step in efforts to attract investment into the project. However, resolving the outstanding land, compensation and financing issues remains critical to translating the latest investment agreement into construction and implementation.

items.title: Dimbaya mobilise les leaders religieux de Kédougou contre les violences
items.description: L’association Agir pour les femmes et les filles de Kédougou (Dimbaya), en partenariat avec Faith to Action Network (F2AN) Afrique de l’Ouest, organise du 19 au 21 octobre un atelier consacré aux droits des femmes et des filles. L’objectif est d’impliquer les leaders religieux et les hommes influents dans la prévention des violences basées sur le genre. Faire des hommes des alliés dans la lutte contre les violences faites aux femmes et aux filles. C’est l’ambition du projet « Ma foi pour la justice de genre ». Pendant trois jours, les participants réfléchissent au rôle des valeurs religieuses dans la promotion du respect, de la dignité et de l’égalité. Pour Abdoul Fatahi Alitchawu, chargé de projet à F2AN Afrique de l’Ouest, les guides religieux, très écoutés dans les communautés, peuvent contribuer à faire évoluer les comportements. « La promotion des droits des femmes et des filles nécessite l’implication des hommes, particulièrement des leaders religieux », souligne-t-il. La présidente de Dimbaya, Sadio Diouara, insiste également sur la nécessité d’une participation active des hommes. Pour elle, la lutte contre les violences ne peut réussir sans leur participation active. L’objectif est de susciter une prise de conscience et de former des hommes capables de porter des messages de sensibilisation dans leurs communautés. L’atelier prévoit notamment d’identifier des enseignements du Coran et de la Bible favorables aux droits humains, puis d’élaborer des messages de sensibilisation destinés aux mosquées, aux églises et aux quartiers. À l’issue des travaux, quinze leaders religieux seront sélectionnés pour devenir des relais communautaires. Ils devront diffuser les messages de prévention et encourager des changements durables. Le choix de Kédougou tient aussi aux défis liés à sa situation frontalière et à l’exploitation aurifère, qui exposent certaines femmes et filles à des risques de vulnérabilité et de traite des personnes. Amadou DIOP (Correspondant)

items.title: Massacre du 17 octobre 1961 : le dérapage méprisant d’un candidat à l’Élysée
items.description: David Lisnard, maire de Cannes, est candidat à l’élection présidentielle française de 2027. Pour faire parler de lui, l’homme sait chasser sur le terrain du courant dominant du moment, l’extrême droite, du moins en ce qui concerne l’Algérie. Lundi soir sur LCI , celui qui est considéré comme proche de Sarah Knafo, la numéro deux de Reconquête, le parti de l’extrémiste Éric Zemmour, a livré une réponse lunaire et choquante sur le massacre du 17 octobre 1961 à Paris, qui a coûté la vie à des centaines de manifestants algériens. Adjoint de Bruno Retailleau au parti Les Républicains jusqu’en mars dernier, il n’est pas étonnant que Lisnard tienne de tels propos sur l’Algérie. Le massacre du 17 octobre 1961 ? « Je m’en fous, je n’étais pas né » Interrogé sur le plateau de LCI par une étudiante sur le massacre du 17 octobre 1961 , dont le 65e anniversaire a coïncidé avec la mobilisation des Français contre la vie chère de samedi dernier, Lisnard a eu une réponse sèche, mêlée d’agacement. « Je m’en fous, je n’en ai rien à foutre, j’en ai rien à cirer, j’étais pas né », a-t-il dit. L’étudiante qui soulevait le sujet a tenté d’expliquer ce qu’il s’est passé il y a 65 ans à Paris : une manifestation pacifique d’Algériens contre un couvre-feu, suivie d’une répression policière violente qui a fait un carnage. Comment peut-on livrer une telle réponse quand on parle de centaines de morts, de surcroît quand on est candidat à la présidentielle ? Selon lui, les Algériens « sont passés à autre chose », et il n’y a donc pas lieu d’en parler. « Il y a eu l’indépendance de l’Algérie. J’ai des potes algériens, heureusement mes potes d’origine algérienne, ils ont bien compris qu’on était passé à autre chose », a tenté d’argumenter celui qui est par ailleurs le président de l’association des maires de France et fondateur du mouvement Nouvelle Énergie. « On ne prétend pas diriger la France en méprisant une partie de ses morts » Devant l’insistance de l’étudiante, Lisnard a fini par concéder tout juste que ce qui s’est passé « c’est très grave, c’est dramatique, mais c’était en 1961 ». Évidemment, la scène est très commentée. Livrer une telle réponse quand on parle de « dizaines de morts, noyés dans la Seine », c’est du « racisme décomplexé », a jugé sur X le député de La France insoumise (LFI), Thomas Portes. « On ne prétend pas diriger la France en méprisant une partie de son histoire et de ses morts », a répliqué pour sa part la députée écologiste Sabrina Sebaihi, qui rappelle que le 17 octobre 1961, « des centaines d’Algériens manifestant pacifiquement ont été tués à Paris, certains jetés dans la Seine ». Mme Sebaihi avait porté une proposition de résolution pour la reconnaissance officielle de ce massacre, adoptée en mars 2024 par l’Assemblée nationale française. Antécédents racistes Dans la foulée, les antécédents racistes de David Lisnard ont refait surface. « Le raciste Lisnard ne peut pas représenter les maires de France. Nous attendons leurs réactions », a affirmé sur X le député LFI Paul Vannier, en partageant des captures d’écran de tweets remontant à 2010 et 2011. « Je ne comprends rien aux préceptes de l’islam, je suis hallalphabète », écrivait par exemple David Lisnard il y a une quinzaine d’années. Ou encore : « Le gouvernement annonce qu’il va réprimer les Roms. Ça fera des vacances à mes clients arabes. » « Je ne comprends pas : l’Histoire qui compte ne commence-t-elle qu’après notre naissance ? Et 1939, 1914, 1870, 1789 ? Étions-nous déjà de ce monde ? Et si nos enfants le disaient comme ça, “rien à cirer, je n’étais pas né”, comment réagirions-nous ? », a répliqué le journaliste François Clémenceau. L’article Massacre du 17 octobre 1961 : le dérapage méprisant d’un candidat à l’Élysée est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: Ghana now facilitates 40% of Burkina Faso’s petroleum transit – Jinapor
items.description: Ghana is facilitating the transportation of approximately 40% of Burkina Faso’s petroleum products, up from 15% two years ago, Minister for Energy and Green Transition, Dr John Abdulai Jinapor, has disclosed. He disclosed in a Facebook post on Tuesday, October 20, 2026, following a courtesy call by a delegation from Burkina Faso’s national petroleum company, Société Nationale Burkinabè d’Hydrocarbures (SONABHY). The delegation was led by the company’s newly appointed Chief Executive Officer, Forogo Patrice, who expressed appreciation to the Government of Ghana for its continued support in facilitating the procurement and transit of petroleum products through the country. According to Dr Jinapor, the delegation called for deeper collaboration to strengthen the existing partnership between the two countries. The meeting also explored opportunities to improve cooperation in petroleum transportation and supply, deepen regional energy collaboration and advance shared priorities for the mutual benefit of Ghana and Burkina Faso. The increase from 15% to approximately 40% in the share of Burkina Faso’s petroleum products transported through Ghana over two years highlights the growing importance of Ghana’s transit arrangements to Burkina Faso’s fuel supply chain. The engagement is expected to provide an opportunity for both countries to explore further cooperation in petroleum logistics and regional energy supply, building on their existing partnership.

items.description: More than 200 residents of Techiman have benefited from a free health screening exercise organised by the KGL Foundation as part of activities marking Breast Cancer Awareness Month. The outreach, organised in collaboration with Koranteng Memorial Clinic and AgricoHub, offered screening for breast cancer, blood pressure, Human Papillomavirus (HPV), hepatitis B and C, and eye conditions, among other services. Organisers said the initiative was intended to promote early detection and preventive healthcare while making screening services more accessible to residents. Programmes Manager of the KGL Foundation, Nii Ankonu Annorbah-Sarpei, said the exercise went beyond breast cancer screening to give participants an opportunity to assess their general health. “We’re not just covering breast screening; we’re also checking people’s general well-being, specifically ear screening, eye testing, and blood pressure,” he said. He said the initiative targeted the general public, particularly young people and women, while encouraging both men and women to take breast health seriously. Chief Executive Officer of Koranteng Memorial Clinic, Elizabeth Korsah Koranteng, stressed the importance of early screening for timely diagnosis and treatment. “Breast cancer can financially derail you, so it’s important to screen for early detection, diagnosis, and treatment,” she said. She also cautioned against misconceptions about breast cancer, including the belief that the disease was a curse, and urged the public to seek accurate health information and medical attention early. Health and economic productivity Chief Executive Officer of AgricoHub, George Antwi Boasiako, said the partnership was also intended to highlight the connection between good health and economic productivity. “We believe that while you focus on your business and business growth, it is important to look at your health and wellbeing, which is why we are collaborating with KGL Foundation for the health outreach,” he said. “The idea is that you should be healthy and able to run your business.” A student who participated in a health screening exercise for the first time said regular checks were important, particularly for students who spend several months in school before returning home. “This is my first time participating in health screening because we will spend more than three months in school before vacation. We need to be healthy to study in school,” the participant said. The student urged others to take advantage of screening opportunities, noting that some illnesses could go undetected without medical tests. “Some illnesses cannot be detected with our physical eyes. It will require medical screening, so I encourage every student to participate in health screening,” the participant said. The outreach also included a blood donation exercise to help replenish supplies for patients requiring blood transfusions.

items.title: Cameroun : Michèle Ndoki met en garde contre la nomination d’un vice-président par autre personnalité que le président en fonction
items.description: © DR Dans une tribune libre rendue publique, l’avocate et femme politique, ancien cadre du Mouvement pour la renaissance du Cameroun donne à lire ce qu’il faut comprendre du défaut de nomination d’un vice-président six mois après la restauration du poste au Cameroun. Lire l’extrait de la tribune ci-dessous. "Pourquoi contre toute logique de l’exécutif le poste est-il encore vacant ? Le gouvernement avait présenté la vice-présidence comme une garantie de continuité. Laisser le poste vacant pendant six mois soulève des questions sur cette justification. Comme je l’écrivais le 21 septembre, le vice-président peut saisir le Conseil constitutionnel de l’empêchement définitif du président. La loi révisée sur le Conseil constitutionnel va plus loin : le vice-président est le seul à pouvoir le faire. Le Conseil statue ensuite à la majorité des deux tiers de ses membres. Biya a passé 73 jours hors du pays cet été, 49 jours en 2024, principalement en Suisse. Une absence n’est pas un empêchement définitif, et seul le Conseil Constitutionnel peut constater un tel empêchement. Mais des absences de plus en plus longues soulèvent des questions légitimes sur l’identité de ceux qui exercent réellement l’autorité présidentielle. Le Vice-président peut soumettre ces questions au Conseil et la tentation est certaine, puisque l’enjeu est la présidence jusqu’en 2032. Autrement dit, nommer un Vice-président revient à se doter d’un rival potentiel. Paul Biya l’a forcément compris. Aujourd’hui tant que le poste de Vice-président reste vacant, personne ne peut constater son empêchement d’exercer ses fonctions : il ne peut les quitter que par démission ou décès. Alors il conserve le poste et laisse d’autres gouverner en son nom. Où cela nous mène-t-il ? Le régime a besoin de deux choses d’apparence contradictoires : aucun vice-président tant que Paul Biya est en vie, et un vice-président déjà en fonction au moment de sa mort, pour « assurer la continuité ». En d’autres termes, si un Vice-président a été « nommé » alors que Paul Biya quitte ce monde mais avant que l’on annonce son décès, les deux préoccupations se trouvent satisfaites : le président actuel peut terminer ses jours en fonctions. En toute sérénité, et le régime ce maintenir après lui. Il ne serait besoin d’aucune élection, un clan, ou tous les clans ensemble, se contenteraient de demeurer en fonction, et l’on dirait aux Camerounais que la Constitution a été respectée. En réalité, il s’agirait d’un coup d’État, et non une transition. Nous sommes donc aujourd’hui devant quatre possibilités : - Paul Biya nomme lui-même un vice-président. Ce serait légal au regard des textes révisés, mais fondamentalement antidémocratique et antirépublicain. - Il peut décéder ou démissionner alors que le poste est toujours vacant. Le président du Sénat, Aboubakary Abdoulaye, assurerait alors l’intérim, et une élection suivrait dans un délai de 20 à 120 jours. C’est la voie constitutionnelle qui rend le choix aux électeurs. Avec dix autres signataires, j’ai demandé qu’elle soit respectée dans une tribune publiée au début de ce mois. - Il peut demeurer en fonction mais dans l’incapacité de gouverner. C’est la situation actuelle : le pays est à la dérive, dirigé par ceux qui signent en son nom. Une implosion est inéluctable à terme, nous sommes de plus en plus nombreux à le pressentir. - Il peut enfin décéder, et un vice-président surgir d’un décret que personne ne l’a vu signer. C’est contre ce scénario que je mets en garde. Que faire ? Nous l’avons dit : faire constater la vacance. Je le répète, n’en déplaise à certains champions du statu quo, ce n'est pas un acte de rupture avec l'ordre constitutionnel : c'est, au contraire, la condition de son plein rétablissement. C'est reconnaître ce que les faits imposent depuis longtemps, et permettre au pays d'entrer enfin dans le processus que sa propre loi fondamentale a prévu pour une telle situation. Qu’on se le rappelle : cette Nation est née d'un partenariat librement consenti, entre deux entités, mais avant tous entre des millions de volontés agissantes. Nos aînés ont arrosé de leur sang cette Terre bénie pour nous obtenir notre indépendance. Cette transition, c’est notre chance de rendre hommage en nous montrant dignes de ce sacrifice ultime. Nous allons donc l’organiser. Ensemble." Michèle Ndoki Cet article Cameroun : Michèle Ndoki met en garde contre la nomination d’un vice-président par autre personnalité que le président en fonction est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

items.title: La Der/Fj octroie 1,7 millions à 5 Gies du département de Louga
items.description: Les groupements d’intérêt économique (Gie) du département de Louga ont bénéficié d’un accompagnement financier de la Délégation générale à l’entrepreneuriat rapide des femmes et des jeunes (Der/Fj). Il s'agit d’un financement de 1 700 000 F Cfr au profit 5 Gie. La cérémonie de remise s’est tenue lundi 19 octobre 2026 à Louga. Ces financements visent à soutenir les femmes et les jeunes pour renforcer leurs activités génératrices de revenus, tout en favorisant leur autonomisation économique. Présidant la rencontre, l’adjoint au préfet de Louga, Ousmane Thioub, a salué les efforts de la Der/Fj en faveur des populations, notamment des femmes et des jeunes, afin de leur permettre de développer leurs activités entreprenariales. Toutefois, l’autorité administrative a invité les bénéficiaires à respecter leurs engagements en matière de remboursement des crédits. “Le remboursement va sans doute permettre aux générations futures de pouvoir également bénéficier des financements”, a déclaré Ousmane Thioub, rappelant que le respect de cette obligation constitue une condition sine qua non à la pérennité du dispositif. Le Dr Abdoulaye Niane a également abondé dans le même sens, en insistant sur l’importance du recouvrement des crédits. “ Nous appelons tous les bénéficiaires à veiller au respect des conditions de remboursement”, a-t-il lancé. Falel PAM

items.title: Government develops roadmap to improve maternal healthcare and hospital bed management
items.description: The Deputy Minister for Health, Dr Grace Ayensu-Danquah, says the government is developing a roadmap to address challenges in maternal healthcare and improve the quality of care across all regions. Speaking before Parliament’s Public Accounts Committee (PAC), she said the roadmap would establish uniform standards of care, quality control and quality assurance to strengthen maternal health services nationwide. Dr Ayensu-Danquah also disclosed that a pilot phase of a technology-driven bed management system had commenced to address shortages of beds in emergency departments. She said all hospitals had established bed management teams to support the implementation of the system, which is expected to improve bed allocation and management and enable hospitals to respond more effectively to emergency cases. The Deputy Minister called for dedicated funding for maternal health, stressing the need for adequate resources to address existing challenges and improve care for mothers across the country. At the same sitting, the Public Accounts Committee announced that it had settled GH¢33,100 in outstanding debts owed to Pantang Hospital as part of its corporate social responsibility commitment. The payment covered GH¢17,000 owed by the Ghana Medical Association and GH¢16,100 owed by the Akuapem South Municipal Assembly for the treatment of people with mental health conditions who had been found on the streets. The committee also heard responses from major health institutions, including Korle Bu Teaching Hospital, Greater Accra Regional Hospital (Ridge), Pantang Hospital and Komfo Anokye Teaching Hospital, regarding infractions identified in the 2025 Auditor-General’s Performance Audit Report on the management of mortuary facilities in public hospitals. The Births and Deaths Registry also provided updates on issues raised in the 2025 Performance Audit Report concerning government efforts to reduce maternal mortality. Meanwhile, the Unified Petroleum Price Fund (UPPF), under the National Petroleum Authority (NPA), told the committee that the use of technology had improved its access to real-time data and enabled better tracking of Bulk Road Vehicle (BRV) movements. The committee ended the hearing after discharging representatives of Metropolitan, Municipal and District Assemblies (MMDAs) because the Administrator of the District Assemblies Common Fund, Mr Michael Harry Yamson, was absent.

items.title: Why Is Strategy So Difficult?
items.description: O ne might think that the meaning of a word as common as strategy is clear, but it is not. The invaluable Oxford American Writer’s Thesaurus inadvertently captures the confusion: “master plan, grand design, game plan, action plan, policy, program, tactics.” But a master plan is something more specific than a grand design, a policy is what should direct strategy, and tactics exist at a level of intentional action below strategy. The muddle becomes serious when applied to strategy’s original and most important field of human endeavor: war. The roots lie in ancient Greek, which is why stratēgos was the word for “general.” Many weighty works on strategy in war make the basic ideas clear, and yet, as one can see from the badly botched American war with Iran, strategy is acutely difficult. Here we have a war in which the United States has the world’s most advanced technology, highly skilled personnel, and well-trained and -staffed organizations. The U.S. is operating in a theater of war that it has studied for many decades, in partnership with Israel—the most militarily advanced country in the Middle East—as well as, more quietly, most of the Gulf States, and it is receiving the tacit support of countries such as Great Britain. Its enemy is poor and corrupt, and recently lost a large chunk of its senior leadership in a series of bombings and assassinations. But the result is, in important respects, a shocking setback, as Iran continues to throttle one of the world’s most important waterways. This article has been adapted from Eliot A. Cohen’s new book, The Strategist: How to Think About War & Politics . This happened not because America’s weapons malfunctioned, its sailors and airmen were incompetent, or the problems were novel and unanticipated. Rather, America’s battlefield reversals represent a strategic failure of an acutely embarrassing kind. Nor is the issue simply incompetent American political leadership, although that has played its role. The history of strategy is a tale of errors, misjudgments, poor assessments, and inadequate follow-through. It was true of the ancient Greeks, when Athens held the high cards in the Peloponnesian War and lost; it was true of Germany and Japan in the two world wars they launched at times and places of their choosing; it is true of Russia today in Ukraine; it is, for that matter, true of the Iranians themselves, who suffered their own strategic failures against Iraq in the 1980s and Israel in recent years. T he seven core questions of strategy may seem extremely simple, and yet they are rarely answered well. The first is What else is going on? Strategy requires its practitioners to orient themselves to the surrounding environment, for almost never is a country simply facing off against another in isolation. When the Trump administration launched the current round of fighting with Iran, it did so having neglected its environment—indeed, in some ways, having made that environment worse. The U.S. had alienated its European allies, whose active help it needed in keeping the Strait of Hormuz open in the face of mine and surface attacks; it failed to prepare the ground with Gulf allies who would be exposed to Iranian attacks; and it underestimated the extent to which Russia and China had put themselves into a deep partnership with Iran, providing targeting intelligence, the components of military systems, and even some weapons. By fixating on the enemy at hand, the administration neglected the context that had shaped everything else. Governments collect a great deal of intelligence about things that can be counted—tanks, ships, missiles. They do a much worse job of answering the second question, which can be derived from an unlikely classic of strategy: the 1969 movie Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid . Paul Newman and Robet Redford play two relatively nonviolent train robbers in the last days of the frontier. One day, as they are holding up a train, a boxcar door slides open and they are pursued by half a dozen men on horseback. Exciting chase scenes ensue as Butch and Sundance try every trick in their extensive playbook to shake them off, but still the pursuit continues. In bafflement, Butch asks Sundance, “Who are those guys?” It is the second great strategic question, and a subtle one. The two robbers knew how many riders were pursuing them and what weapons they carried. They could probably even tell the breed of horses they were riding. But they did not know what made this band of lawmen so much more persistent and so adept in seeing through their dodges—what motivated them, and what that would mean for Butch and Sundance. That sort of intelligence is difficult to come by, particularly if you do not know that that is the information you need. President Trump and his key advisers likely knew little about the leaders of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, who are now their primary opponents. It is clear that they still cannot fathom how their enemy makes decisions. It is not uncommon for Western leaders to underestimate or simply fail to grasp the ideological or religious motivations of their enemies, and that seems to be part of what has happened in the conflict with Iran. But it seems as well that the administration and its advisers misjudged Iran’s preparedness to launch a protracted, complex war in which it would be outgunned but not necessarily outsmarted. [ Eliot A. Cohen: Don’t ask how this war ends ] The problem is probably reciprocal: If Iran’s leaders have taken the so-called TACO bet—“Trump Always Chickens Out”—they have been repeatedly proven wrong, as indeed have been many of Trump’s domestic critics. They may understand Trump, his motivations, his stock of resolve, and his fears as little as he understands them. Or for that matter, as little as the Israelis understood Yahya Sinwar, the leader of Hamas, even though they had had him in their prisons for 10 years, or as little as Americans understood the calculus of Japanese decision makers in the fall of 1941. Sometimes it is possible not even to know who is in charge on the other side. During most of the Vietnam War, American leaders believed that the charismatic Ho Chi Minh or the experienced General Võ Nguyên Giáp were making the decisions. Later they suspected that it was a collective leadership. In reality, the dominant figure was the colorless first secretary of the Communist Party, Lê Duẩn. In the current war, Trump has frequently expressed his frustration at not knowing who is in charge on the other side. What are we trying to do? is the third and most obvious strategic question, perhaps the easiest to pose and the most deceptive. When critics have gone after the Trump administration over the Iran war, they have usually focused on the supposed unclarity of its goals. They have something of a point, but to a more limited degree than one might think. In truth, the setting of goals, although vital, is a murky and shifting enterprise. Carl von Clausewitz, who in his lifetime witnessed numerous strategic defeats as well as the ultimate victory of the allied coalition over Napoleonic France, taught that war is a continuation of policy by other means. It may be the most important teaching to take away from his classic, On War , and is certainly the most memorable. But if the ultimate objectives in war are political, then they also have political characteristics—that is, they may be vague, inconsistent, and above all changeable. George H. W. Bush famously outlined four objectives for American forces in advance of the 1990–91 Gulf War, in an oft-cited example of strategic clarity. A closer look, however, shows that they were anything but clear. The first objective was ensuring the safety of American citizens in the Gulf—but before the bombs fell, that had already been achieved, because the Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein had released his American and European hostages. American citizens—the soldiers, sailors, airmen, and Marines going into Iraq—were the ones endangered by the war. Expelling Iraq from Kuwait was straightforward enough, but restoring the “legitimate government of Kuwait”—a monarchy backed by a citizenry that included scarcely a quarter of the country’s inhabitants—was not. And as the events of the past 35 years have proven, the fourth objective, ensuring the stability of the Persian Gulf, was a pipe dream. Moreover, some of the objectives the United States pursued either were unstated (stripping Saddam of his nuclear program and setting up the conditions for his overthrow) or evolved only in reaction to events on the ground (protecting the Kurdish population in the north and, to some degree, the Shia in the south). This kind of shift in objectives occurs in all wars. Britain entered World War II nominally to save Poland from Germany. It ended up prohibiting Polish troops from marching in the victory parade in London. The United States invaded Afghanistan to destroy al-Qaeda; it ended up attempting to create an Afghan democratic republic. Considered in this light, the Trump administration’s objective-setting in the Iran war, though messy, is not entirely implausible. Clearly, one objective has been to destroy, or at the minimum badly damage, Iran’s nuclear enterprise; another to limit its ability to threaten its neighbors with missile and drone attacks by dismantling some of its key military industries. A third, and the most questionable, seems to have been to overthrow and replace the regime. That last goal is evidently beyond the current reach of the U.S. military, although the other two have been achieved in some measure. As the war has wound on, the administration has reached for other goals, including the bizarre one of keeping “oil and gas cheap for Americans all over the country,” which Vice President Vance has declared now has primacy over avoiding a nuclear Iran. One problem with the Trump administration’s objective-setting is the president’s foolish insistence that he has achieved more than he has: His repeated use of the word obliteration actually obscures some real, if far from absolute, successes in pursuit of his first two objectives. As for the third, it was always bound to be a reach but was not beyond the realm of possibility. The administration’s real failures have come in setting what were essentially defensive objectives in addition to the offensive ones, above all securing the Strait of Hormuz. For the rest, like many administrations before, it has promised much more than war can ever deliver—think of the hubris of the “war to end all wars,” or the objective of ending tyranny. In democratic societies, the temptation to justify the hazards and sacrifices of war with overblown rhetoric and absurd aspirations usually overcomes the good judgment of political and military leaders alike. [ Read: The Middle East still to come ] What are our means? is the fourth question. At a strictly quantitative level it is usually easily answered by counting tanks, missiles, or ships. But those are often the least important variables in the equation. The real variables are whether organizations can do what we want them to do; whether the technical means we have at our disposal are adequate to the task; and whether, if new challenges arise, we have the resources to meet them. The United States entered the current war with limited stockpiles of its most advanced weapons, limited mine-clearing capabilities, and no frigates whatsoever to escort convoys. It had very little in the way of hardened bunkers for its aircraft in the Persian Gulf, and so suffered some shocking losses on the ground to accurate Iranian missiles (possibly guided by Russian intelligence). And the entire campaign has been predicated on expectations about what bombing could do that were at best highly improbable and at worst totally unrealistic. The administration clearly overestimated what the U.S. military could do, but one has to wonder whether the armed forces also misjudged their own capabilities. Decades of underinvestment in both passive defenses (for example, concrete shelters, underground command posts) and active ones (for example, surface-to-air missile batteries), not any particular decision of the Trump administration, have exposed the U.S. Air Force to high losses. A similar decades-long lack of commitment to the counter-mine-warfare and the escort-of-convoy missions has made the Strait of Hormuz operation so difficult. “Know the enemy and know yourself and in a hundred battles you will not be defeated,” goes the saying of the Chinese general Sun Tzu. But military organizations and their leaders frequently fail to understand themselves, and in particular their own weaknesses. America’s lack of preparedness to conduct classical counterinsurgency warfare in Iraq and Afghanistan cost it dearly in blood, money, and time. Most militaries fail to conduct a sober reckoning with their own deficiencies by examining their lack of resources, organizational preparation, or aptitude. The fifth and sixth questions are What is our priority? and In what sequence should we act? For a country as wealthy and powerful as the United States, these are particularly uncomfortable questions. American leaders often act as though their resources are infinite and few really difficult strategic choices need to be made. That flexibility is one of the blessings (and occasionally the curse) of an astoundingly wealthy and populous country. Economists like the word trade-off —to get this, you have to give up that. The military uses instead phrases such as economy of force or acceptable risk that mask the blunter truth that some things are more important than others. In the current Iran war, it has become clear that getting control of the Strait of Hormuz has never been the top priority—had it been so, the U.S. would have conducted a variety of operations, probably including seizing some of the smaller islands near the strait. Setting priorities can be acutely difficult in war. The best decision Franklin D. Roosevelt made during the Second World War was one of priority. Military and political leaders alike had believed in 1941 that Germany would be a more important enemy than Japan and needed to be tackled first. But the war began for the United States with the Pearl Harbor attack of December 7, 1941. Over the next six months, Roosevelt agreed to the British proposal to invade French North Africa in November 1942. General George C. Marshall, the chief of staff of the U.S. Army, and Admiral Ernest J. King, the chief of naval operations, thought it a strategic error and opposed it, favoring instead an invasion of France in 1943. Roosevelt’s calculation was chiefly political: To sustain domestic support for the “Germany first” policy, American forces had to be in action somewhere in the European theater of operations within a year of Pearl Harbor. He got his priorities right, and Marshall and King, who did not think politically, were wrong. (As it happened, a 1943 invasion would probably have been an operational debacle as well for the untried U.S. Army, but that was a separate matter.) If Roosevelt got priority right, however, he got sequencing wrong. Like most politicians, he did not want to feel trapped by prior decisions—what political scientists call “path dependence.” He believed that he could have the North Africa invasion and still invade France in 1943, and he was wrong. The defeat of German armies in North Africa took longer than expected, and was not completed until March 1943. Sicily loomed as an easy target, and besides, shifting large forces to Britain, particularly before the U-boat menace in the Atlantic was defeated, would take time, so in July the Allies attacked the island and took it. That triggered the fall of the Italian dictator Benito Mussolini; the logical next Allied move was therefore a landing in Italy. That occurred in September 1943, in the immediate aftermath of Italy’s defection from the Axis. And that, in turn, led to a swift German occupation of Italy and an ensuing front in Europe that no one had anticipated. [ Timothy W. Ryback: How Hitler dismantled democracy in 53 days ] Sequencing, then, was only partially under Roosevelt’s control, or anyone else’s for that matter. One thing led to another, and as is so often the case in war, the contenders looked as though they were playing chess one move at a time, seizing an opportunity without fully anticipating the consequences of doing so. The final question is in many ways the most difficult: What is our theory of victory? Or, put more simply, Why do we think this will work? In the case of the Iran war the theory of victory seems to be: We will inflict so much economic pain on the regime that it will give in, either because it will hate to see the Iranian economy ruined or because its people will rise up and overthrow it . But Iran has been suffering self-imposed economic misery for decades, and its leaders, with their own corrupt networks, can live in splendor while others suffer. And as for an uprising, the time to support that would have been when Iranians took to the streets in December and January 2026, before 30,000 were massacred by the Islamic Republic’s repressive apparatus. If there is any theory of victory left for the United States, it is that more reasonable Iranian leaders will replace the extremists—but it would appear at the moment that the hardest of the hard-liners are the ones with the guns. Articulating a theory of victory is no different from constructing a plausible story—the different characters find themselves in a situation, they do this and that, and there is an outcome. In practice, though, such theories are rarely offered in governmental deliberations—and here I speak from personal experience. I saw that play out while sitting in the Situation Room as senior officials discussed sending more soldiers, or diplomats, or aid money to Afghanistan, without anyone quite broaching the question of how the moves under consideration were supposed to lead to success. Such failures are entirely common, as the perusal of archival records confirms. Strategy is chiefly about execution—the exceedingly complicated and difficult task of moving forces from one place to another, guiding them through combat, and responding to unforeseen circumstances. There are ancillary activities—diplomatic initiatives, the public presentation of the reasons for war or expositions of why it is going the way it is, the gathering and deployment of financial and industrial resources. All of this requires serious, detailed, and extremely consequential work. To begin telling a story, or even to ask for one, in such a circumstance can seem frivolous at best, and at worst downright subversive of the efforts officials are investing and the sacrifices soldiers are making. Why is it all so hard? One reason lies in the sheer uncertainty of all wars, in which personalities, contingent events, accidents, bloodlust, shifting political calculations, and sheer good or bad luck play their part. But no less important are the weaknesses of the decision makers themselves. For one, they are often, if experienced, old and suffering the afflictions of age, or if young, inexperienced and either cocky or timid. Historians will parse the records of the Trump administration or, like the cardiologist of the late Vice President Dick Cheney, wonder what it meant that the president was clearly in poor physical and possibly mental health. He would hardly be alone. Prime Minister Anthony Eden launched the Suez operation of 1956 against Egypt’s Gamal Abdel Nasser. At the time, he had been hospitalized with a fever of up to 106 degrees following a set of badly botched gallbladder operations. He had been taking amphetamines and sleeping pills. In a fascinating study of Eden, David Owens, himself a former foreign secretary and a physician, concluded that Eden’s physical health played a large role in the poor decision making that helped produce a major debacle. Roosevelt was on the edge of death in the last year of World War II; Winston Churchill had a heart attack; and Joseph Stalin, in addition to suffering from hypertension, had become increasingly paranoid. John F. Kennedy took a horrifying cocktail of drugs for his bad back and suffered from Addison’s disease. Woodrow Wilson had an incapacitating stroke that left the U.S. government largely in the hands of his protective wife. These are not isolated cases. Even healthy younger leaders may find themselves suffering from acute sleep deprivation and other disorders. A flattering portrayal of President Biden’s national security adviser noted that, during the American withdrawal from Afghanistan in 2021, Jake Sullivan was getting two hours of sleep a night for days on end. As those who have studied medical residents know, going that short of sleep practically guarantees poor decisions. The psychologist Daniel Kahneman and his colleague Amos Tversky have examined many heuristic shortcuts that distort rational decision making. Almost all of them apply in strategic decision making as well. Take anchoring, our tendency to judge an event, problem, or cost based on some existing piece of information. The trivial case is the extremely expensive bottle of wine put on a restaurant menu with the idea of making the second- or third-most-expensive bottle look reasonably priced. Strategic anchoring occurs frequently. In the run-up to the German invasion of the Soviet Union in June 1941, not only Hitler but also his generals concluded that Russia was a fragile giant. They anchored their perceptions on the 1939–40 winter war between the U.S.S.R. and Finland, when 200,000 Soviet troops were killed, wounded, or captured by Finnish militiamen. They paid no attention to the way in which the Soviets had learned swiftly from their failures in that war, and did not account for all of the advantages that Russians would derive from fighting on their own ground. In a similar vein, both the Russian military and Western observers anchored their perception of Ukrainian fighting power in the 2014 and 2015 rounds of conflict in the Donbas as well as the Russian seizure of Crimea. They had discounted, or simply ignored, the improvements in Ukrainian training and equipment since then, or, in parallel with the 1941 case, the differences that would emerge when Ukrainians were fighting to protect their villages and cities from an army that would commit rape and murder with abandon. Strategic decision making is rarely a matter of individual choices; more often it is the result of some kind of deliberation. This is true even in the most extreme totalitarian countries. Stalin called the shots, but Marshal Georgy Zhukhov could get a hearing. This leads to another obstacle to sound strategic judgment: collective pathologies. The phenomenon described by Irving Janis as groupthink applies particularly forcefully to strategic decision making: illusions of invulnerability, collective discounting of warnings, unquestioned belief in one’s own inherent morality, stereotyped views of adversaries, self-censorship, and the exclusion of dissidents, or their reduction to marginal status. Lyndon Johnson heard out George Ball, the in-house dissenter on Vietnam, and then moved swiftly on. These and many other pathologies have beset not only the Trump administration in Iran, but most countries at war. They can be mitigated but not resolved. Formal procedures are less helpful than qualities of character. Of these the most important are empathy, to understand both the enemy and one’s own side; curiosity, because every war is new and distinctive; humility, to accept that one has made mistakes; and above all moral courage, to face facts for what they are and to make decisions accordingly. The president is singularly deficient in all of these aspects. He finds it difficult to imagine the world as seen by others; he seems to be incurious about the important details of military operations; he is far from humble; and if he is averse to anything, it is admitting that he might be wrong. These traits do not seem, moreover, to be confined to him but are shared by many in his administration. [ Listen: The ‘great man’ presidency ] The strategic virtues, to be clear, are rarely found. But they do exist. Churchill, whose courage was justly famous, was a great war leader. He benefited as much, however, from his empathy as from his courage. His great advantage over Hitler, as the historian John Lukacs has shrewdly noted, is that he could imagine what it was like to be Hitler, but Hitler could never imagine what it was like to be Churchill. One cannot study Abraham Lincoln’s conduct of the Civil War without being struck by his curiosity and humility—neither of which interfered with his resolve and decisiveness. Nor is it the acknowledged great figures of history alone who show these qualities: When President George W. Bush made the call in December 2006 to surge forces to Iraq despite the apprehensions of his military and political subordinates, he exhibited considerable moral courage. Israeli Prime Minister Levi Eshkol made a number of decisions in the run-up to the Six-Day War that bought Israel at least a modicum of the support and understanding that it would need from abroad, and which, in very different circumstances, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has so profligately squandered. Some view strategy as so difficult that it is not even worth attempting. These are not only counsels of despair but of nihilism. Some decision makers have shown excellent strategic judgment and used war to achieve their political objectives. The most notable might be Anwar Sadat, the long-underestimated Egyptian president who launched the 1973 Yom Kippur War and used a spectacular early success that could have easily ended in catastrophe to secure the peace he wanted. War is a hideous thing. There are even more hideous things, however, as anyone who has visited the mass graves of Sarajevo or the slaughter field of Bucha in Ukraine will know. A war with Iran now may well be far less terrible than a war launched by an Iran with nuclear weapons later. Moreover, sometimes war is unavoidable: True pacifists are few, and no nation committed to pacifism has survived the predations of a hostile neighbor that is not. The chances are good that anyone reading this article lives in a country that is currently at war, or has been at war, or is closely affected by war. It is a near certainty that they live in a country whose borders have been shaped by war, and quite probably one whose form of government has resulted from war. All of us therefore have, or should have, a keen interest in strategy. Unfortunately, however, its practice will not get any easier in the future. War is spreading to new domains, and employing new and terrible conventional weapons, many capable of acting on the basis of decisions that machines will make in fractions of a second. Nuclear weapons are spreading, and we now face the potential of devastating biological weapons manufactured with the aid of artificial intelligence. The previous experiences and professional knowledge of generals and admirals becomes ever more swiftly obsolete; the hazards of untried political leaders wading through such uncertainty, immensely greater. More countries have the capacity to do terrible things, and are seemingly willing to do so. None of that is an excuse for neglecting the subject that Aristotle thought essential for a citizen. In his Rhetoric , he talks at length about the subjects an orator must master, including “the military strength of his country, both actual and potential, and also the nature of that strength; and further, what wars his country has waged, and how it has waged them. He must know these facts not only about his own country, but also about neighboring countries; and also about countries with which war is likely, in order that peace may be maintained.” Strategy is one of the oldest of subjects. It is powerfully shaped by current events and technologies but best learned through a deep encounter with the history of war. It can be studied but rarely mastered, and it is the domain of both calculation and inevitable error. Of one thing we can be certain: As we look at a world in which violence is not the last resort for many countries and organizations hostile to our values and interests, and may very well be the first, strategy will be needed more than ever. This article has been adapted from Eliot A. Cohen’s new book, The Strategist: How to Think About War & Politics .

items.title: A New Season of Autocracy in America
items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts In this new season of Autocracy in America , host Anne Applebaum sits down with leaders in politics, technology, and culture to discuss what can be done now to reverse the slide toward autocracy. The following is a transcript: Anne Applebaum: The midterms mark the beginning of the end of President Donald Trump’s second term in office. Although we don’t know who and what the results will bring, we do know that, regardless of what happens, there will now be opportunities to prevent the further degradation of our democracy. This November, the Autocracy in America podcast is coming back, this time to focus on that recovery. I’m Anne Applebaum of The Atlantic . Join me for interviews with the people who will be leading the charge. I’ll talk with leaders about their plans to work with the administration, to restore international relationships, and to repair the damage done to our economy. I’ll ask what it could look like to retrain and restrain ICE, rescue our cultural institutions, and keep our elections safe. The new season of Autocracy in America arrives Tuesday, November the 10th, and will be available in video and audio. Subscribe on YouTube or wherever you get your podcasts.

items.title: US: Order ‘No ICE’ Zones during Election Period
items.description: Click to expand Image A voter carries a ballot during early voting in the New York City mayoral elections on October 25, 2025. © 2025 Olga Fedorova/AP Photo (Washington, DC) – The United States government should order federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers not to operate in the vicinity of polling places, early voting locations, or drop boxes during the midterm electoral period, Human Rights Watch said today. The presence of these federal agents could deter people from voting. “ICE officers’ abuses have already seriously affected US citizens who have been stopped, beaten, detained, deported, and even killed,” said Philippe Bolopion, executive director at Human Rights Watch. “Voters should not have to fear being caught in an ICE dragnet when they head to the polls.” In-person early voting is already taking place in the majority of states. In a nationwide September poll, 40 percent of respondents said they expect some kind of ICE presence at polls, with even higher percentages among non-white respondents expecting to see ICE agents in places people vote. Federal law generally prohibits federal officials from sending “troops or armed men” to voting sites. Several state laws prohibit any armed officers, including police, from engaging in acts that could interfere with the elections or intimidate voters by their presence near polling places. Some states bar law enforcement officers, including police, from being in close proximity to polling places at all unless they are responding to a specific incident. Despite these robust prohibitions, neither President Donald Trump nor the heads of the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and the Federal Bureau of Investigation have been willing to rule out the possibility that federal agents, including ICE, may be at places where people vote. In March, then-Deputy Attorney General and now-Attorney General Todd Blanche said, “Why is there an objection to sending ICE to polling stations? ... Illegals can’t vote. It doesn’t make any sense.” In February, Karoline Leavitt, who was White House press secretary at the time, said she could not “guarantee” that ICE agents won’t be around a polling location in November. In early September, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there were no plans to station ICE agents at polling places but left the door open for them to be there if “serving a warrant on someone that we have been actively tracking down” or if “there is a threat to that polling place.” Three lawsuits are pending in federal courts to prevent ICE from operating at the polls, with an additional court case seeking to require the government to disclose its plans regarding ICE agents at polling places. In Washington, DC, the Board of Elections in October asked the National Guard to limit their presence near drop box locations for the midterm election following complaints that troops had been spotted near a drop box in Foggy Bottom. The Trump administration has long touted the idea that large numbers of noncitizens unlawfully cast ballots in US elections but has not produced any evidence suggesting that the problem exists at a scale that would have affected the result of any election, anywhere in the country. Multiple research studies, including from the Fair Elections Center, Bipartisan Policy Center, Brennan Center, and the Cato Institute, have found no evidence of mass voting by noncitizens and concluded that the problem is insignificant in electoral outcomes. ProPublica found that federal immigration officers have detained at least 500 US citizens since the start of Trump’s second term, including 36 incidents in which detained US citizens were prevented from contacting their family or lawyers for 24 hours or more. The same study also found that agents who questioned their claims of citizenship detained more than 100 US citizens, nearly all of them people of color. In Minnesota, Human Rights Watch found that ICE’s Operation Metro Surge abuses terrified many people, causing them to stay home and miss work, school, and even essential health care appointments. US citizens of color whom Human Rights Watch interviewed at the time said they were so fearful of racial profiling that they began carrying their passports everywhere. Human Rights Watch analysis also suggests that in 2025, ICE used race and ethnicity in Los Angeles as a crude proxy for identifying a person’s nationality, and detained people on that basis. Perceptions of the risks associated with an encounter with ICE may well be higher among non-white communities. The notoriety of those incidents and of ICE’s widespread abuses over the last two years risks dissuading some people from voting if they feel they are likely to encounter ICE agents near polling places, Human Rights Watch said. “ICE agents should be publicly ordered to stay away from the polls and anywhere ballots are being cast,” Bolopion said.
